          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. On the last date of hearing, i.e., 17.11.2026, on behalf of
the Board, we were furnished with a chart highlighting project and
non-project land inventory valuation.  In the said chart, the
details of non-project land - unencumbered were furnished, as well
as the details of non-project land - encumbered were furnished. Few
other details were also furnished in the said chart.
2. All the learned counsel appearing for the lenders wanted to
verify whether they have any stake to put forward insofar as non-
project land, i.e., unencumbered land is concerned. This non-
project land - unencumbered is shown at serial nos. 1.1 to 1.11 in
the chart.
3. Today, when the matter was taken up for further hearing, the
learned counsel appearing for the lenders brought to our notice
that there is no problem insofar as lands at serial nos. 1.1 to
1.10, respectively, are concerned. They need to undertake some
inquiry as regards the land at serial number 1.11 is concerned.
They would undertake the inquiry and come back to this Court with
an appropriate report. For the sake of convenience, we set out the
entire  list  of  project  and  non-project  land  inventory  -
23

1 Non-Project Land – Unencumbered
1.1 Agra Budhera
     245.69 
      
104.03 
 
 1,228.45 
Government  of  Uttar  Pradesh  came  out
with a Policy for Development of 06 Hitech
Townships in the state  vide its Policy of
2003.  Unitech  was  selected  as  a
Developer for two such Hitech Townships
at  Agra  and  Varanasi.  Each  of  these
townships were to be developed over an
area of 1500 acres in phases,  minimum
being  300  acres  in  phase  -1.  The  2003
Policy provided that land for the Township
would  be  acquired  by  the  State
Government  or  any  of  its  agencies.  It
included  certain  incentives,  the  most
important being exemption from payment
of Stamp Duty, and exemption from the
provisions of land ceiling law (i.e. Section
154  (2)  of  the  Uttar  Pradesh  Zamindari
Abolition  and  Land  Revenue  Act,  1950.
The  State  Government  unilaterally
modified the said Policy in the years 2006
and 2007 whereby the state Government
backed out from acquisition of land for the
project and this was left to the Developer.

homebuyers,  through  their  bank  accounts,  upon  verification  of
documents and submit compliance report before the Hon’ble Court.”  
11. The total amount to be paid to these 07 eligible customers
comes to Rs.3,25,89,184/-. Registry shall disburse this amount,
lying in SLP (Crl.) Nos. 5978-5979/2017 in favour of the Board for
the purpose of disbursement to the 07 customers named above.
12. I.A. no.355188/2026 is at the instance of one of the home-
buyers. The applicant claims to be an allottee of Apartment
No.0203, Second Floor, Tower 21, Unitech Horizon, Plot No. 6,
Sector  Pi-2,  Alistonia  Estate,  Greater  Noida,  Uttar  Pradesh
(Customer Code UZ0920). The flat was allotted on 08th May, 2006. The
applicant has stated on oath that he has paid Rs.43,18,272/-. He
was to take possession by 15th November, 2008. In the application,
the applicant has prayed for the following:-
“a. permit the Applicant to intervene in Civil Appeal No. 10856
of 2016;
b. direct the Board of Unitech Limited to file a status report on
Apartment No. 0203, Second Floor, Tower 21, Unitech Horizon,
Greater Noida, stating its availability, and the Applicant's
statement of account and balance dues (if any);
c. permit the Applicant, as a one-time individual measure on
medical and humanitarian grounds and notwithstanding the cut-off
of 31.10.2025, to change his option from refund to possession of
Apartment No. 0203, Second Floor, Tower 21, Unitech Horizon,
Greater Noida (Customer Code UZ0920);
d. direct the Board to hand over possession of the Apartment No.
0203, Second Floor, Tower 21, Unitech Horizon, Greater Noida to
the Applicant, within such time as this Hon'ble Court may fix,
and to execute the conveyance deed in his favour as and when
34

## Page 71

registration is permitted for the project; or, if the apartment
is not available, to allot him an equivalent completed, lift-
served apartment in the same project;
e. direct that, pending disposal of this application, the
Apartment No. 0203, Second Floor, Tower 21, Unitech Horizon,
Greater Noida shall not be cancelled, re-allotted or encumbered;
and 
f. pass such other order as may be just and appropriate in the
facts of the case.”
Heard the learned counsel appearing for the parties. In the
peculiar facts of this case, more particularly, having regard to
the averments made in paras 5, 7 & 8, respectively, we are inclined
to grant the relief prayed for in this application. Paras 5, 7 & 8,
respectively reads thus:-
“5. That Mrs. Ruby Gupta has thus lost both legs below the knee
and her right arm below the elbow, and gangrene has also affected
the fingers of her remaining left hand. She depends on others for
movement and for every daily activity. She remains on long-term
medication  and  requires  regular  follow-up,  wound  care  and
physiotherapy, as advised at her discharge.
xxx 
7. That Mrs. Ruby Gupta presently resides at 3/27, 1st Floor,
Roop Nagar, Malka Ganj, Delhi 110007, in a building with no lift.
With both legs amputated, she cannot use the stairs at all, and a
wheelchair cannot be taken up or down them. She must be carried
up and down the stairs for every hospital visit and for any
movement outside the house, and is, in effect, confined indoors.
Her treating doctor has advised a lift-served residence with
access to open areas.
8. That the need for a lift-served residence is grave and
immediate. Every hospital visit means carrying Mrs. Ruby Gupta
down and up a flight of stairs. The Applicant, now aged 59, finds
this increasingly beyond her (sic) strength, and each such trip
endangers her safety. Her isolation within the house compounds
her depression. A residence with a lift is the only arrangement
35

## Page 72

that will allow her to leave her home safely and with dignity,
and to receive the medical care she needs.”
13. We once again clarify that this order shall not be cited as a
precedent. In the peculiar facts, more particularly, having regard
to the averments made in the three paragraphs above referred to
above, we have granted this indulgence. The I.A. No.355188/2026
stands disposed of accordingly.
14. As regards what we have observed in para 16 of our order dated
17th  November,  2026,  we  need  some  update  from  the  Police
Commissioner. We request the Police Commissioner, Gautam Buddh
Nagar to join the proceedings online on the next date of hearing,
i.e., on 09th December, 2026. We expect the Police Commissioner to
now take appropriate steps at the earliest for removal of each and
every encroachment. How to do it, is for the Police Commissioner to
plan it out.
15. Mr. Harish Pandey, the learned counsel has appeared today on
behalf of the Police Commissioner, Gautam Buddh Nagar. We have made
it very clear today that by 09th December, 2026, each and every
encroachment/ unauthorized construction has to be removed from
these parcels of land. On 09th December, 2026, Mr. Harish Pandey
will  inform  us  about  the  action  taken  and  the  removal  of
encroachment.

O R D E R
By order dated 16.02.2026, Special Leave Petition (C) Nos. 8044-
8045/2025 were disposed of with the following order:
“Having considered the matters, we do not find any infirmity
in the impugned order warranting interference by this Court.
Accordingly, the Special Leave Petitions stand dismissed.
2. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
3. Having said that we cannot be oblivious to the fact that in
the present case, the petitioner was able to construct a G+1
floor building without any sanction plan being approved. It
speaks volumes about the conduct and the responsibility of
the Municipal Corporation, which is required to be aware of
the  developments  on  the  ground  and  also,  is  required  to
ensure  that  no  violation  of  any  rules  and  regulations  or
requirement relating to construction is made. A full one and a
half storied building getting constructed and not even noticed
by the Authorities and only thereafter, an order is passed for
demolition  by  the  very  same  Authorities.  It  indicates  an
alarming state of affairs as the same could not have been done
without  the  collusion  and  connivance  of  the  Municipal
Authorities. Accordingly, we direct the State Government to
1

## Page 101

conduct a thorough inquiry, as to why, such incidents occur
where entire structures are completed without due sanction
from  the  proper  authorities,  including  the  Municipal
Corporation, without any resistance or corrective measures
being taken by them to prevent such constructions. 
4.  Before  deciding  the  future  course  of  action,  let  learned
counsel for the Municipal Corporation submit a report, as to
why, the situation has been allowed to develop in the manner
it has. The report to be submitted by respondent no.2 by filing
a personally affirmed affidavit within three weeks. 
5. List on 25.03.2026.”

5. Respondent No.1 - State of Tamil Nadu is directed to file an

6. From the facts emerging in the present proceedings, and
from similar matters coming before this Court, it is evident
that there are apparent widespread and blatant violations of
building bye-laws and land-use regulations. Constructions are
frequently undertaken in blatant violation of the applicable
norms  and  regulations,  including  in  the  prohibited  areas.
More importantly, upon completion, such lands and buildings
are often put to uses other than those for which sanction was
originally granted by the competent authority.
7. We have also been coming across cases where residential
colonies  are being  converted into  commercial  areas  by  the
unauthorised  use  of  residential  buildings  and  lands  for
commercial purposes. Such practices are not only contrary to
law  and  public  interest,  but  also  cause  significant
inconvenience and prejudice to bona fide residents, who have
invested  substantial  resources  in  purchasing  property  and
constructing  their  houses.  The  environmental  and  civic
consequences of such misuse by unscrupulous elements of
society are equally serious and have far-reaching implications.
8. In view of the above, we deem it appropriate to examine the
issue on a pan-India basis.
9. Accordingly, all Municipal Corporations and Municipalities,

3. Thereafter, these matters have been listed on subsequent dates
5

## Page 105

and several directions have been issued. 
4. Be that as it may. By the order of the Hon’ble Chief Justice of
India, the matter has been listed before this Bench. 
5. We  have  perused  the  issues  sought  to  be  taken  up  in  this
Miscellaneous  Application.  Although,  the  main  matter  has  been
dismissed, we find there is a practical difficulty in considering this
Miscellaneous Application further “on a pan-India basis by impleading
all Municipal Corporations and Municipalities of the capital cities of
all the States and Union Territories as party respondents.” 
6. We say so for the reason that every State and Union Territory has
its respective Municipal Laws and bye-laws which are unique to each
State and Union Territory. The Bye-laws/Regulations with regard to
construction of buildings in the capital cities of all the States and
Union Territories are distinct. It is neither practical to pass common
orders  applicable to  all  the  States  and  Union  Territories nor  is it
feasible to go into the issue concerning breach of building bye-laws
while putting up construction or  carrying out repairs of buildings
State-wise by this Court and further on a case to case basis. 
7. Owing to the pendency of this Miscellaneous Application before
this Court, there is a  proliferation of litigation before this Court by
6

## Page 106

filing of Writ Petitions and/or applications in this very case. Further,
these  Special  Leave  Petitions  which  have  already  been  dismissed
cannot be permitted to be continued as a Public Interest Litigation on
a pan-India basis where orders are being sought in private interest.
Hence,  we  find  that  the  compass  of  this  matter  will  have  to  be
circumscribed. 
8. Therefore, we say that all pending applications before this Court
in this matter seeking whatever relief are to be disposed of and are
disposed of with liberty  to  the  parties to  approach  the concerned
authorities - Municipal Corporations or Municipalities, Tribunals or
the High Court, as the case may be, for seeking appropriate directions
to be issued in respect of their individual cases.
9. Therefore,  we  state  that  any  action  taken  by  the  authorities
pursuant to the order passed in this Miscellaneous Application may be
challenged  before  the  appropriate  authorities  or  the  Court,  if  so
advised.
10. The pendency of this matter before this Court would not come in
the way of the Municipal Corporations and other allied authorities
acting in accordance with law.
11. At this stage, we wish to make certain observations. 
7

## Page 107

12. A city is a shared civic space and not merely an aggregation of
individual property entitlements. It is sustained by municipal rules
and regulations, including construction and building bye-laws of each
State and Municipal Corporation/Municipality. The violation of these
laws, regulations and bye-laws causes immense damage to the city’s
civic infrastructure including its roads, drainage, and traffic capacity. 
13. All  persons  have  civic  obligations.  The  Fundamental  Duties
embodied  in  Article  51A  of  the  Constitution  of  India  collectively
articulate a vision of responsible citizenship. Respect for constitutional
institutions [Article 51-A(a)] and the pursuit of excellence in collective
life [Article 51-A(j)] are values antithetical to the casual disregard of
laws designed for the common good. For immediate reference they are
extracted as under:
“51A. Fundamental duties.- It shall be the duty of every
citizen of India – 
(a) to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and
institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem;
xxx
(j) to strive towards excellence in all spheres of individual
and collective activity so that the nation constantly rises
to higher levels of endeavour and achievement.”
14. The 74th amendment to the Constitution which has incorporated
Chapter IXA has to be borne in mind. The relevant provision of the
8

## Page 108

same is extracted as under:
“243W.  Powers,  authority  and  responsibilities  of
Municipalities,  etc.- Subject  to  the  provisions  of  this
Constitution, the Legislature of a State may, by law, endow –
(a) the Municipalities with such powers and authority as may
be necessary to enable them to function as institutions of
self-government and such law may contain provisions for
the  devolution  of  powers  and  responsibilities  upon
Municipalities,  subject  to  such  conditions  as  may  be
specified therein, with respect to -
(i) the  preparation  of  plans  for  economic
development and social justice;
(ii) the  performance  of  functions  and  the
implementation of schemes as may be entrusted
to them including those in relation to the matters
listed in the Twelfth Schedule;
(b) the Committees with such powers and authority as may be
necessary to enable them to carry out the responsibilities
conferred upon them including those in relation to the
matters listed in the Twelfth Schedule.
xxx
Twelfth schedule
(Article 243W)
(1) Urban planning including town planning.
(2) Regulation of land-use and construction of buildings.
(3) Planning for economic and social development.
(4) Roads and bridges.
(5) Water supply for domestic, industrial and, commercial
purposes.
(6) Public health, sanitation conservancy and solid waste
management.
(7) Fire services.
9

## Page 109

(8) Urban  forestry  protection  of  the  environment  and
promotion of ecological aspects.
(9) Safeguarding the interests of weaker sections of society,
including the handicapped and mentally retarded.
(10) Slum improvement and upgradation.
(11) Urban poverty alleviation.
(12) Provision  of  urban  amenities  and  facilities  such  as
parks, gardens, play-grounds.
(13) Promotion  of  cultural,  educational  and  aesthetic
aspects.
(14) Burials  and  burial  grounds;  cremations,  cremation
grounds and electric crematoriums.
(15) Cattle ponds; prevention of cruelty to animals.
(16) Vital  statistics  including  registration  of  births  and
deaths.
(17) Public amenities including street lighting, parking lots,
bus stops and public conveniences.
(18) Regulation of slaughter houses and tanneries.”
15. Compliance  with  building  regulations,  is  in  a  sense,  an
elementary expression of civic responsibility by both citizens as well as
Municipal  Authorities  at  all  levels.  We  are  disturbed  to  note  their
flagrant violation throughout the country. 
16. The Constitution of India envisions citizenship as participation in
a common civic enterprise. Our  cities, in turn, demand the same
compact from  citizens, namely, that  private  ambition  must remain
10

## Page 110

within public limits. 
17. At the same time, we are also conscious that the rule of law is
rendered hollow when the authority charged with enforcing it does not
enforce it. The state of municipal inspection in our cities, for example,
is  in  shambles,  to  say  the  least.  It  is  often  undertaken  after  the
building has risen and the violation has become a fait accompli. Such
inspections are, to say the least, a sham. It is also an open secret that
unauthorised construction often flourishes with the active connivance
of  municipal  authorities  hoping  that  State  Governments  would
ultimately  “regularise”  the  same,  particularly  before  an  impending
election.  
18. We are also not oblivious to the fact that the chronic congestion
of  our  principal  cities  and  the  proliferation  of  unauthorised
construction  therein  is  symptomatic  of  the  extraordinary  pressure
upon  land  and  infrastructure  in  this  Country.  Our  urban  policy
permits  population,  employment,  commerce  and  governmental
functions to become excessively concentrated in a handful of centres.
Our  state  capitals,  in  particular,  cannot  indefinitely  bear  the
cumulative  burden  of  being  simultaneously  administrative
headquarters,  economic  magnets,  employment  centres  and
destinations for every conceivable public and private activity. The time
11

## Page 111

has come, therefore, for building more cities in the Country. We don’t
need to expand our  existing  cities either  vertically  or  horizontally,
particularly, State capitals but to build new cities and townships, in
order  to  distribute  people,  opportunity  and  public  and  corporate
administration across a wider landscape. It is indeed sad that in a
Country as big as India, only a handful of cities sustain most part of
economic  activity.  Therefore,  decongestion  is  indispensable  to  the
preservation of liveability in our principal cities and the same can be
attained only by building more cities and townships. Decongestion of
large metros, State capitals and cities is the need of the hour. Building
new cities and spaces would not only reduce pressure on existing State
capitals and cities but also generate employment opportunities and
thus be a catalyst for economic development. It is high time that the
Central and State Governments devote their attention on this aspect of
governance. Any future planning of new cities must bear in mind the
likely  increase  in  population  and  accordingly  seek  to  build
towns/cities with a futuristic vision and in a sustainable manner.  
19. In the circumstances, we think that the issues which have arisen
in  this  Miscellaneous  Application  have  to  be  limited  to  seeking
suggestions from the respective State Governments which would be
filed before this Court by means of an affidavit of the concerned and

Leave granted.
2. Briefly stated, the facts of the case are that the
appellant herein is stated to be a small manufacturing
enterprise, whereas the respondent is a Government of
India undertaking incorporated under the provisions of
the Companies Act, 1956 and is, inter alia, engaged in
the business of setting up power plants and equipment. 
2.1 Between the years 2011 and 2014, the appellant
received several purchase orders from the respondent
1

## Page 127

for the supply of Solar Power Conditioning Units and
items  relating  to  SPV  Wind  Diesel  Power  Plants.
Pursuant thereto, eight contracts came to be executed
between  the  parties.  Subsequently,  the  respondent
alleged that the appellant had failed and/or neglected
to complete the work in respect of certain items and,
accordingly,  withheld  payment  pertaining  to  such
unfinished work.
2.2 Aggrieved by the withholding of payments, the
appellant preferred an application dated 29.08.2017
under  Section  18  of  the  Micro,  Small  and  Medium
Enterprises Development Act, 2006 (for short, “the
MSMED Act, 2006”) before the West Bengal State Micro
Small  Enterprises  Facilitation  Council.  The
Facilitation Council initiated conciliation proceedings
under Section 18(2) of the MSMED Act, 2006, of which
the respondent was duly informed. However, despite two
hearings  being  conducted,  the  respondent  did  not
participate  in  the  conciliation  proceedings.
Consequently, the conciliation failed, which was duly
communicated  to  the  parties,  and  the  matter  was
2

## Page 128

referred for arbitration under Section 18(3) of the
MSMED Act, 2006, giving rise to Case No. 107 of 2017.
2.3 The  Arbitral  Tribunal,  vide award  dated
24.09.2019 passed in Case No. 107 of 2017, allowed
the claim of the appellant and awarded a sum of Rs.
61,08,654/-, together with interest at three times
the bank rate notified by the Reserve Bank of India,
compounded with monthly rates, in terms of Section 16
of the MSMED Act, 2006. The appellant was further
directed to submit the computation of interest on the
principal  amount,  duly  quantified  by  a  Chartered
Accountant, along with its claim for the principal
amount.
2.4 Aggrieved  by  the  aforesaid  award,  the
respondent  instituted  Arbitration  Petition  No.
AP/175/2020 before the Calcutta High Court, seeking to
set aside the arbitral award dated 24.09.2019. The
respondent also filed an application, being GA No. 1 of
2020  in  AP/175/2020,  under  Section  36  of  the
Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, seeking stay of
3

## Page 129

operation of the said award. On the other hand, the
appellant  instituted  Execution  Application  No.
EC/156/2020 before the High Court, seeking execution of
the arbitral award.
2.5 The High Court, by order dated 01.09.2021,
disposed  of  GA  No.  1  of  2020  in  AP/175/2020,
directing the respondent to deposit 75% of the total
awarded amount, comprising the principal amount and
interest quantified by the Chartered Accountant at
Rs. 2,78,88,228/-. The respondent was directed to
deposit 50% of the aforesaid amount in cash with the
Registrar, Original Side of the High Court within
three weeks and furnish a bank guarantee from a
reputed bank for the remaining 50% within the same
period.
2.6  Subsequently,  respondent  filed  another
application, being GA No. 3 of 2020 in AP/175/2020,
under Section 16 of the Arbitration and Conciliation
Act, 1996, seeking stay of operation of the arbitral
award  dated  24.09.2019,  as  well  as  the  execution
4

## Page 130

proceedings in EC/156/2020. The appellant, on the
other hand, filed GA No. 1 of 2020 in EC/156/2020,
seeking release of the amount already deposited by the
respondent, having regard to its precarious financial
condition.
2.7 On 06.12.2021, the learned Single Judge of the
High Court released the matter in view of the pendency
of the review petition. Thereafter, on 07.02.2022, the
Hon’ble Chief Justice of the High Court, in exercise of
his administrative powers, assigned the matter to a
particular learned Single Judge for consideration of
all the pending applications. 
2.8     The High Court, by order dated 23.03.2022,
allowed GA No.1 of 2020 in EC/156/2020, filed by the
appellant and permitted it to withdraw 75% of the
principal amount awarded by the Arbitral Tribunal
within a period of two weeks, without furnishing any
security. By the same order, GA No.3 of 2020 in
AP/175/2020 filed by respondent was also allowed and
the operation of the arbitral award dated 24.09.2019
5

## Page 131

was  stayed  until  the  disposal  of  the  pending
proceedings.
2.9 Aggrieved  by  the  aforesaid  order,  the
respondent herein preferred an appeal under Section 37
of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, being
APO/41/2022 in EC/156/2020, before the Division Bench
of the High Court. The respondent also filed GA No. 3
of  2021  in  AP/175/2020  before  the  learned  Single
Judge, seeking stay of the order dated 23.03.2022,
insofar it permitted the appellant to withdraw 75% of
the principal amount awarded by the Arbitral Tribunal.
By order dated 28.03.2022, the learned Single Judge
stayed the operation of the order dated 23.03.2022,
until  01.04.2022,  observing  that,  in  view  of  the
appeal preferred by the respondent, the question as to
whether the stay ought to be extended was to be
considered by the Appellate Court.
2.10 Thereafter, the learned Single Judge of the
High Court, by judgement and order dated 29.03.2023,
dismissed AP/175/2020 and upheld the arbitral award
6

## Page 132

dated 24.09.2019. The learned Single Judge also imposed
a cost of Rs. 5,00,000/- on the respondent for the
protracted litigation.
2.11 Aggrieved  by  the  aforesaid  judgement  and
order, the respondent preferred another appeal under
Section 37 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act,
being APO/85/2023 in AP/175/2020, before the Division
Bench of the High Court. In the said appeal, the
respondent, inter alia, contended that the dispute in
question was a commercial dispute within the meaning of
the  Commercial  Courts  Act,  2015  and  that  the
proceedings had been adjudicated by a learned Single
Judge who was not designated as a Commercial Court
under  Section  4(2)  thereof.  It  was,  therefore,
contended that the judgement and order passed by the
learned  Single  Judge  was  without  the  requisite
jurisdiction.
2.12 The Division Bench of the High Court, by the
impugned judgement and order dated 13.05.2026, disposed
of  APO/41/2022  arising  out  of  EC/156/2020  and
7

## Page 133

APO/85/2023 arising out of AP/175/2020/. The Division
Bench set aside the judgement and order passed by the
learned Single Judge dated 29.03.2023 on the ground of
lack of jurisdiction. It was observed that, on the date
of  institution  of  the  proceedings  challenging  the
arbitral award, the value of the award exceeded rupees
two crore and therefore, the proceedings ought to have
been instituted before the Commercial Division of the
High Court. However, neither of the parties had taken
steps to have the proceedings under the Arbitration and
Conciliation Act, 1996 transferred to the Commercial
Division.
2.13 The  Division  Bench  further  observed  that
although the Chief Justice of the High Court had
assigned the proceedings to the learned Single Judge,
the said Judge was not designated as a Commercial Court
under Section 4(2) of the Commercial Courts Act, 2015,
either on the date of such assignment or on the date of
passing of the judgement and order dated 29.03.2023.
Accordingly, the Division Bench held that AP/175/2020
could not have been adjudicated by the non-commercial
8

## Page 134

division of the High Court. Consequently, in exercise
of powers under Section 15(5) of the Commercial Courts
Act,  2015,  the  proceedings  in  AP/175/2020  and
EC/156/2020 were directed to be placed before the
Commercial Division of the High Court for consideration
in accordance with law.
3. Being  aggrieved  by  the  order  dated  13.05.2026
passed by the Division Bench of the High Court of
Calcutta (Civil Appellate Jurisdiction) (Original Side)
in APO/41/2022 and APO/85/2023 by which the appeals
filed  under  Section  37  of  the  Arbitration  and
Conciliation Act, 1996 (hereinafter referred to as the
“Act” for the sake of brevity) were allowed and the
matter(s) was remanded to the learned Single Judge of
the Commercial Division for the purpose of rehearing
the application filed under Section 34 of the said Act,
the appellant(s) is before this Court.
4. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant
and learned counsel for the respondent. We have perused
the material on record.
9

## Page 135

5. Admittedly, the respondent herein preferred the
application under Section 34 of the Act by invoking
the Ordinary Original Civil Jurisdiction of the High
Court as against an interim order passed in the said
matter as AP/175/2020 along with EC/156/2020 which
was an execution proceeding were assigned by the
Hon’ble Chief Justice of Calcutta High Court to the
learned  Single  Judge.  For  ease  of  reference,  we
extract the Assignment Order related to the Original
Side by the Chief Justice of the Calcutta High Court
dated 07.02.2022 which is an administrative order by
the Master of the Roster as under:

10

## Page 136

6. By notification dated 11.11.2025 issued by the
order of the Acting Chief Justice of the Calcutta
High Court by a deeming fiction, the exercise of
jurisdiction by Benches, not being a Regular Bench of
Commercial Division of the High Court, has to be
construed to be exercising powers under Commercial
Courts Act, 2015. The said notification reads as
under:
“IN THE HIGH COURT OF CALCUTTA
NOTIFICATION
No. 7438-RG Dated 11/11/2025
It is to be hereby notified to all concerned
that the Hon’ble Bench/Benches, not being a
Regular  Bench  of  Commercial  Division  or
Intellectual Property Rights Division of this
Court,  while  taking  up  ‘Part-Heard’  and/or
‘Specially Assigned’ matters arising out of
such  Divisions,  shall  be  deemed  to  be
exercising  the  jurisdiction  and  powers
conferred on those Hon’ble Benches under the
Commercial Courts Act, 2015 and Intellectual
Property Rights Division Rules of the High
Court  at  Calcutta,  2023  and  relevant
Rules/Practise  Direction  to  hear  up  the
matters.
By  Order  of  the  Hon’ble  the  Acting  Chief
Justice
Sd/-
Registrar General,
High  Court  at
Calcutta”
11

## Page 137

7. The learned Single Judge accordingly heard the
application under Section 34 of the Act and dismissed
the  same.  Being  aggrieved,  APO/41/2022  and
APO/85/2023 were filed before the Civil Appellate
Jurisdiction  (Original  Side)  by  the  respondent
herein. 
8. Having filed the application under Section 34 of
the  Act  before  the  Ordinary  Original  Civil
Jurisdiction and no objection being raised with regard
to the jurisdiction of the learned Single Judge to
hear the said application, on being unsuccessful, the
appeals were preferred by the respondent(s) before the
Civil Appellate Jurisdiction on Original Side. It is
for the first time before the Division Bench that a
contention was raised by the respondent herein with
regard to the jurisdiction of the learned Single judge
to hear the application under Section 34 of the Act.
The Division Bench of the High Court held that the
learned Single Judge who had been assigned the matter
by the Chief Justice had no jurisdiction whatsoever
and consequently, set aside the order passed by the
12

## Page 138

learned Single Judge and has now remanded the matter
to the Commercial Division of the High Court for being
heard afresh on merits. It is the said order of the
remand which has been assailed before this Court.
9. We find that the Division Bench of the High Court
was not right in allowing the appeals and setting
aside the order passed under Section 34 of the Act by
the learned Single Judge and thereby remanding the
matter  to  learned  Single  Judge  of  the  Commercial
Division to rehear the application under Section 34
afresh. 
10. Firstly, the respondent herein had preferred the
application under Section 34 of the Act before the
Ordinary Original Civil Jurisdiction of the High Court
and not the Commercial Division. Having filed the said
application  under  the  said  jurisdiction  and  the
occasion arising to allot this matter to a particular
Bench, the Chief Justice of the High Court allotted the
matter to a learned Single Judge on the Original Side.
The said assignment was made by the Chief Justice of
13

## Page 139

the High Court in exercise of his powers as Master of
the Roster and on the Administrative Side. Once the
said assignment was made before  particular learned
Single Judge there was no contention raised with regard
to the jurisdiction of the learned Single Judge to hear
the said matter as assigned. It is only when the
respondent herein was unsuccessful before the learned
Single  Judge  and  the  appeals  were  filed  invoking
Section 37 of the Act before the Division Bench that
the issue regarding the jurisdiction of the learned
Single Judge to adjudicate upon the matter was raised
by the respondent herein. The Division Bench was of the
opinion that the matter could not have been heard by
that particular learned Single Judge in the Ordinary
Original Civil Jurisdiction and the assignment had to
be made to the Commercial Division of the High Court.
Hence, the matter has been remanded by the Division
Bench of the High Court. 
11. We observe that once the Master of the Roster,
namely, the Chief Justice of the High Court had made
an assignment to a learned Single Judge of the High
14

## Page 140

Court to hear a particular case by Special Orders, no
objection could have been raised to the same before
the  Division  Bench  of  the  High  Court  in  appeal
particularly when such an objection was not raised
before the learned Single Judge by the respondent
herein.
12. We note that the respondent herein who did not
raise any objection whatsoever to the learned Single
Judge  being  assigned  with  the  case  hearing  the
application under Section 34 of the Act strangely
raised objections to the same before the Division Bench
of the High Court. In fact, the discussion in the
impugned  judgment  proceeds  on  the  basis  of  the
objections raised by the respondent herein.
13. We find that in the facts of this case, the
Division Bench of the High Court has ignored the fact
that the Chief Justice as the Master of the Roster had
assigned this particular case to the learned Single
Judge on the Original Side. This was precisely because
the respondent had filed the application under Section
15

## Page 141

34 of the Act invoking the Ordinary Original Civil
Jurisdiction of the High Court and not under the
Commercial Division of the High Court. Therefore, it
was not expected that the Chief Justice would have
assigned this matter to the Commercial Division Bench.
Hence, the justification offered by the respondent that
the matter had to be heard by the Commercial Division
and by the Judge presiding in the Commercial Division,
cannot be accepted.
14.  The Division Bench of the High Court ought to
have  noted  the  fact  that  there  was  a  specific
assignment of this case to a particular Judge by the
Chief Justice of the High Court on the administrative
side as the Master of the Roster and that ought to have
been  respected.  In  the  above  circumstances,  the
impugned  order  is  set  aside,  APO/41/2022  and
APO/85/2023 are restored on the file of the Division
Bench of the High Court. We request the Division Bench
to now hear the appeals on merits as expeditiously as
possible  and  dispose  of  the  same  on  merits  in
accordance with law.
16

## Page 142

15. However, we refrain from imposing costs on the
respondent.
16. The appeals are disposed of in the aforesaid
terms.
Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. We have today before us one interim application filed by   
Mr. Amar Jain.  In the interim application, the applicant has 
prayed for the following:-
“a) Direct the Union of India and the concerned states
and Union Territories to comply with the directions as
regards the appointment of Commissioners for Persons with
Disabilities contained in order dated 29.07.2026 within a
time-bound manner, as fixed by this Hon’ble Court and to
file a compliance affidavit in this regard
b) Direct the appointment of a State Commissioner for
Persons with Disabilities with Independent Charge in
Jammu and Kashmir, within a time-bound manner, as fixed
by this Hon’ble Court”
2. Mr.Rahul Bajaj, the learned Advocate and Mr. Amar Jain
(on line) joined the proceedings & brought to our notice the
9

## Page 154

W.P.(C) No.  243/2005
order  passed  by  this  Court  dated  29.07.2026,  more
particularly, the observations made in paragraphs 9, 10,
11,12 and 13 respectively, are concerned.  We  quote  the
relevant observations as under:-
“9. Mr. Bajaj pointed out that the State Governments are
obliged to appoint Commissioners in accordance with the
mandate of Section 79 of The Rights of Persons with
Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016. According to him, the State
Commissioners have an important role to play for better,
effective,  and  meaningful  implementation  of  various
provisions of the Act. He pointed out that the following
States have yet to appoint State Commissioner:
i)  Delhi,  ii)  Haryana,  iii)  Rajasthan,  iv)  Himachal
Pradesh, v) Karnataka, vi) Andaman and Nicobar Islands,
(vii) Nagaland, viii) Puducherry, ix) Sikkim, x) Tamil
Nadu.
10. We direct all the States referred to above to ensure
that the Commissioners are appointed in accordance with
Section 79 of the RPWD Act within a period of four weeks
from today. This direction shall be strictly complied with
and none of the States referred to above should exhibit
any laxity in this regard. The laxity, if any, shall be
viewed very strictly.
11.  It is needless to clarify that the State concerned
shall appoint the Commissioner with an independent charge.
The State should not appoint anyone as a Commissioner
holding additional charge. 
12. Mr. Bajaj also pointed out that there is no full-
time Chief Commissioner for persons with disabilities
since 2019. It is the Secretary in the DEPwD who is
holding this post as an additional charge. This, according
to him, is in the teeth of the note to Rule 30 of the RPWD
Rules 2017. As according to Mr. Bajaj, the Rule requires
10

## Page 155

W.P.(C) No.  243/2005
any Government servant to resign from Government service
on taking charge as CCPD. The Chief Commissioner and two
Additional Commissioners have to be appointed as per the
mandate of Section 74 of the RPWD Act.
13. We direct the Union to ensure that the appointments
of Chief Commissioner and two Additional Commissioners in
accordance with Section 74 of the RPWD Act are undertaken
within a period of four weeks from today. We invite the
attention of the Union to Rule 30,  of the Rules which
reads thus:
“30.  Qualification  for
appointment  of  Chief
Commissioner.
- No person shall be eligible for
appointment  as  Chief
Commissioner, unless -
(a)  he  is  a  Graduate  from  a
recognized  University:  Provided
that preference shall be given to
persons having recognised degree
or diploma in social work or law
or management or human rights or
rehabilitation  or  education  of
persons with disabilities;
(b) he is having experience of at
least  twenty-five  years  in  a
Group  "A"  level  post  in  the
Central  Government  or  a  State
Government  or  a  public  sector
undertaking or a semi Government
or  an  autonomous  body  dealing
with disability related matters
or social sector or as a senior
level functionary in registered
national  and  international
voluntary  organizations  in  the
field  of  disability  or  social
development:
Provided that out of the total of
twenty-five years of experience,
he  should have  at least  three
years of experience in the field
of rehabilitation or empowerment
11

## Page 156

W.P.(C) No.  243/2005
of persons with disabilities; and
(c) he has not attained the age
of sixty years as on 1st January
of the year of recruitment.
Note. - If he is in the service
under the Central Government or a
State Government, he shall seek
retirement  from  such  service
before  his  appointment  to  the
post.”

IA Nos.99054/2024 and 99055/2024
1. Pursuant  to  our  order  dated  03.09.2025  passed  in  these
applications, a joint meeting of the TTZ Authority and CEC was
convened. The TTZ Authority has consequently filed an affidavit
dated 30.10.2026, stating, inter alia, that in the meeting held on
22.09.2026,  attended  by  representatives  of  CEC  and  NEERI,
permission was granted for the development of the IMC project in
Villages Raipur and Rahankalan, Tehsil Etmadpur, District Agra,
subject  to  thirteen  conditions.  These  conditions  have  been
reproduced in paragraph 5 of the Note submitted by the learned
Amicus Curiae. During the course of the hearing, however, our
attention was drawn to an email dated 06.11.2026 addressed to the
TTZ Authority by Mr. A.K. Mohanty, Member, CEC, and Expert Member,
TTZ  Authority,  expressing  certain  reservations  regarding  the
decision purportedly taken in the aforesaid joint meeting. The
reasons underlying these apprehensions have been duly incorporated
4

## Page 165

by the learned Amicus Curiae in paragraphs 9 to 12 of the report.
2. In these circumstances, we are of the view that a fresh joint
meeting between the TTZ Authority and CEC is necessary to resolve
the outstanding issues and arrive at a considered and coordinated
decision. Let the meeting be held, and a joint report be submitted
to this Court within three weeks.
3. Post on 17.12.2026.
IA Nos. 243178 of 2026 and 275202 of 2026
4. Let these applications be forwarded to the CEC for its
consideration and appropriate recommendations.  
IA Nos.292695/2026
5. Post on 05.01.2027.
IA No.344174/2026
6. The  learned  Additional  Solicitor  General  of  India,  on
instructions, informs us that the authorities concerned are willing
to comply with the recommendations made by CEC in its Report No.63
of 2025.   Learned Amicus, on instructions from the CEC, states
that necessary permission for felling of trees may be accorded,
subject to the condition that the authorities concerned shall give
prior intimation to the Divisional Forest Officer, who shall ensure
that felling of trees is undertaken under his direct supervision.
IA Nos.351366/2026 and 352878/2026 
7. These  applications  have  been  filed  by  Powergrid  Ghiror
Transmission Limited (PGTL), seeking permission of this Court for
5

## Page 166

the installation of two Inter-State Transmission System lines meant
to evacuate 3.5 GW of renewable energy from the the Rajasthan

inspections on 30.07.2026 and again from 21-23.09.2026, with the
Conservator of Forests, Agra and other officials of the forest
department. Consequently, the CEC has submitted Report Nos. 30 and
31 of 2026, both dated 28.10.2026, recommending permission for: (i)
felling of 83 trees and lopping/light pruning of 400 trees in
connection with the 765 kV D/C Dausa–Ghiror transmission line; and
(ii) felling of 187 trees and lopping/light pruning of 210 trees in
connection with the 400 kV D/C Ghiror–Firozabad transmission line.
The permission has been granted subject to the following conditions
contained in paragraph 10 of CEC Report No. 30 of 2026 and
paragraph 9 of CEC Report No. 31 of 2026:
“30. Vide Report No. 30 of 2026 dated 28.10.2026, CEC has
recommended as follows in paragraph 10 of the Report:
10. Considering the national importance of the proposed 765
kV  D/C  Dausa-Ghiror  Transmission  Line,  an  Inter-State
Transmission  System  project  intended  to  facilitate  the
evacuation of 3.5 GW of renewable energy from Rajasthan REZ
Phase-IV, CEC after the site visits and careful examination
of all relevant records, recommends that this Hon’ble Court
may kindly consider granting permission for felling of 83
trees and lopping/light pruning of 400 trees falling within
the TTZ in connection with the aforesaid transmission line,
in place of the 297 trees originally proposed for felling and
1,735 trees originally proposed for lopping/pruning, subject

i) felling of the 83 trees, comprising 67 trees in Agra
District and 16 trees in Firozabad District, shall be carried
out strictly under the supervision of the Uttar Pradesh
Forest  Department,  and  the  Applicant  shall  bear  the

8. In view of the recommendations made by CEC and the submissions
of the learned  Amicus Curiae, we are inclined to allow these
applications  subject  to  the  compliance  with  the  above-stated
conditions imposed by CEC.  We, however, clarify that PGTL is
permitted to undertake the plantation of trees during the ensuing
rainy season. The felling of trees can be initiated once the
applicant furnishes an undertaking that all conditions imposed by
the CEC, including those relating to compensatory afforestation,
shall be complied with.  A compliance report shall be submitted to
the  CEC,  which  shall  verify  compliance  with  the  stipulated
conditions and, if considered necessary, submit a further report to
this Court.
I.A. Nos. 237739/2024 and 237765/2024 
9. These applications were filed by certain persons alleging,
inter alia, that during the intervening night of 18-19.09.2024,
more than 300 fully grown trees were felled using JCB machines at
Dalmia Farm, Chhatikara Road, Vrindavan, District Mathura. It was
alleged that the trees were felled without any prior permission
from this Court or from the competent statutory authority under the
Uttar Pradesh Protection of Trees Act, 1976.  The incident also led
to the registration of FIR No. 413/2024 under various provisions of
the Indian Forest Act, 1927. The applicants accordingly sought
9

## Page 170

investigation from an independent agency to assess the number of
trees felled and the extent of damage to the environment, to
suggest appropriate restoration measures; compensatory plantation
of 100 trees for every tree illegally felled, and to constitute a
committee to monitor the implementation of the Urban Greening
Guidelines, 2014 in Vrindavan.  Pursuant to the directions issued
by this Court, the CEC conducted a site inspection and submitted
Report No. 29 of 2024, revealing that a total of 454 trees were
felled. Of these, 422 trees stood on approximately 14.88 hectares
of private land known as Dalmia Farm. While the other 32 stood on
the adjoining roadside strip, which forms part of a protected
forest. There were certain other findings as well recordings the
use of JCB machines and chain saws to carry out felling of trees.
10. The CEC thereafter submitted another Report No. 35 of 2024,
i.e., the final report, making the following recommendations:
a) A penalty of a minimum of Rs. 1,00,000/- (Rs. One lakh
only) per tree felled and removed without the prior
permission of this Hon’ble Court shall be imposed on the
land owner. Hence for 454 trees felled and removed without
the prior permission of this Hon’ble Court a minimum
penalty of Rs.4,54,00,000/- (Rs Four Crores Fifty-four
lakh only) shall be imposed on the land owners. The amount
shall be deposited with the Forest Department for taking
up new plantations at suitable places in TTZ.
b) The Forest Department shall also recover the requisite
penalty due under the provisions of the UP Protection of
Trees Act, 1976 for this illegal felling.
c) The Forest Department should take punitive action against
the land owners for felling 32 trees that were standing in
the Protected Forest as per the provisions under the
Indian Forest Act 1972.
d) An  entry  path  to  the  extant  private  land  has  been
constructed through the protected forest. Hence Forest
Department  shall  initiate  action  under  the  Forest
10

## Page 171

Conservation Act 1980 for illegal breaking of land without
prior permission of the Central Government.
e) The area be restored by planting 422 trees on the private
land and 32 trees in the protected forest area at the cost
of the land owner.
f) The  Forest  Department  shall  plant  and  maintain  4540
saplings of Indigenous species (ten times the number of
trees felled as per norms applicable for compensatory
plantation in TTZ) and another 4540 as penal compensatory
plantation (ten times the number of trees felled without
the prior permission of this Hon’ble Court) i.e. a total
of 9080 saplings at the cost of the land owners, at any
nearby place to be provided by land owner which is
suitable for plantation. This land shall also be declared
as the Protected Forest by the State Government.
g) The entire timber illegally felled shall be confiscated by
the Forest Department and disposed of as per the norms of
the UP Forest Department.
h) The Mathura Vrindavan Development Authority should ensure
that no construction of any sort takes place at that part
of the extent site where the Forest Department will do the
Plantation.
i) The Chairman, TTZ authority shall ensure compliance of all
the conditions/penalties that may be imposed by this
Hon’ble Court. The Chairman, TTZ authority shall intimate
such compliance to the CEC on a quarterly basis till all
conditions imposed by this Hon’ble Court are complied
with.
j) This Hon’ble Court may consider imposing any other penalty
for the contempt of this Hon’ble Court committed by the
land owners by felling the trees without seeking prior
permission of this Hon’ble Court.
11. This Court, vide order dated 16.12.2024, relied upon the
recommendations made by the CEC and issued contempt notice to
Shankar Agarwal alias Shiv Shankar Agarwal, the alleged contemnor.
Directions were also issued to the Forest Department to act on
clauses (b), (c), (f) and (g) of the Report No. 35 of 2024 of CEC,
and to close the entry path referred to in clause (d) of the said
report. Certain other directions were also issued to the Forest
11

## Page 172

Department, including maintenance of status quo in all respects
regarding the subject property. Notice was also issued to Mathura
Vrindavan Development Authority to ensure compliance with the
recommendations contained in the aforesaid CEC report.
12. This Court,  vide order dated 25.03.2025 recorded that the
alleged contemnor had admitted on affidavit that 454 trees had been
felled without prior permission of this Court. Certain punitive
directions were also issued.
13. It is not in dispute that in deference to those directions
following  compliances  and  developments  have  taken  place:  (i)
penalty of Rs. 4.54 crores has been deposited vide DD No. 033038
dated 21.04.2025 with the Divisional Director, Social Forestry
Division, Mathura.  (ii) Complaint dated 13.12.2024 is pending
before Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate-I (ACJM-I), Mathura,
and a revision petition arising therefrom is pending before the
Sessions Judge-III, Mathura. (iii)  A separate complaint dated
24.12.2024 with respect to felling of 32 trees under the Indian
Forest Act and unauthorized creation of an entry path through the
protected forest, is also pending before ACJM-I, Mathura.  (iv)
For the restoration of 454 trees, a sum of Rs. 52,03,500/- has been
deposited on 20.01.2026 for undertaking plantation in the upcoming
rainy season.  (v)  In relation to the proposed plantation of 9,080
saplings, 9.46 hectares of land have already been registered in the
name of the Forest Department on 06.01.2026. A further sum of Rs.
2,55,23,800/- has been deposited on 20.01.2026 towards plantation
and maintenance for a period of ten years.  (vi)  The Timber
12

## Page 173

recovered at the site has been confiscated and auctioned through
Uttar Pradesh Van Nigam.  (vii)  Mathura Vrindavan Development
Authority vide letter dated 23.01.2026 has informed that the area
is under constant vigilance, that no construction exists at the
site and that no construction will be allowed either.  Similarly,
quarterly reports have also been filed. As regards to the question
of further penalty, the matter has been left to the discretion of
this Court.
14. In  light  of  the  aforesaid  developments,  we  find  that
substantial compliance has been made with directions issued by this
Court insofar as the contemnor is concerned. We are, however, of
the view that the following additional directions are necessary:
(i) The land provided by the contemnor measuring 9.46 hectares, and
now registered in the name of the Forest Department, shall be
notified as forest land. Let the needful steps be taken in this
regard within 8 weeks.
(ii)  The Forest Department shall submit a compliance report
regarding the plantation undertaken pursuant to the directions of
this Court to the CEC. Upon receipt thereof, the CEC shall conduct
a spot inspection to verify compliance and submit a further report
to this Court.
(iii)  The penalty amount of Rs.4.54 crore shall be utilized , in
the first instance, towards plantation of trees as per the orders
of this Court. Any unutilized amount shall be earmarked for the
afforestation activities in the Mathura-Vrindavan area.  In the
13

## Page 174

event the amount has already been utilized, a compliance report,
indicating the details of such utilization, shall be filed.
15. The  only  issue  that  now  survives  for  consideration  is
imposition of any further penalty upon the contemnor.  We have
considered the submissions made by the learned  Amicus Curiae as
well as learned counsel appearing for certain intervenors, who
strongly urged that the contemnor deserves to be strictly dealt
with and adequate punishment be imposed by way of imprisonment
keeping in view the nature and manner in which the offence was
committed. 
16. On the other hand, Mr. Mukul Rohatgi, learned Senior Counsel
representing the contemnor, points out that he has already remained
in custody for more than thirty days. He further points out that a
substantial penalty has already been imposed and duly deposited by
the contemnor. In these circumstances, he urges this Court to take
a lenient view.
17. Upon consideration of the rival submissions, it seems to us
that no further incarceration of the contemnor is warranted. The
ends of justice would be adequately met by imposing a lump-sum
penalty  of  Rs. 50,00,000/-  (Rupees  Fifty  Lakh  only)  on  the
contemnor.  The contemnor is directed to deposit the aforesaid
amount in the following manner: 
(i) A sum of Rs. 20 lakhs shall be deposited with a government-
owned and government-run institution engaged in the welfare of
destitute persons and widows residing in Mathura-Vrindavan area.
14

## Page 175

(ii) A sum of Rs. 10 lakhs shall be deposited with a government-
owned and government-run institution engaged in the welfare of
persons with disabilities.
(iii)  A sum of Rs. 10 lakh shall be deposited with a government-
owned and government-run institution providing care and shelter to
orphaned children.
(iv)  A sum of Rs. 10 lakh shall be deposited with a government-
owned and government-run institution for providing first-aid and
medical assistance to pilgrims visiting the Mathura-Vrindavan area.
18. Let a compliance report in this regard be filed, failing which
the contempt proceedings shall stand revived.
19. Upon deposit of the entire amount of Rs. 50 lakh with the
institutions specified hereinabove and due compliance with these
directions, the contempt proceedings shall stand dropped. The order
directing maintenance of status quo in respect of the subject
property shall also stand vacated.
20. This order shall have no bearing on the pending criminal
complaints or any other proceedings arising out of the incident.
IA Nos.331428/2026 (in Suo Moto W.P. (Civil) No. 8/2026)
21. Let CEC submit a report within four weeks.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following 
                             O R D E R 
1.This order is in continuation of the previous orders dated 
31.08.2026 and 27.10.2026 passed by this Court, whereby the 
Union of India was called upon to explain why a complete 
prohibition on the retail sale of acid ought not to be 
imposed. The Union of India was also granted time to place on 
record an affidavit setting out the reasons for permitting the 
continued retail sale of acid in the open market, as well as 
the measures proposed to be undertaken by the State 
authorities to prevent its misuse. 
7

## Page 196

 
2.We have briefly heard the Petitioner in Person, learned 
counsel for the parties and the learned Amicus Curiae. 
3.At the outset, the intervenor-NGO, namely, NAVYA Centre for 
Justice and Social Change, through Dr. Navpreet Kaur, had 
earlier submitted a ‘Comprehensive Survivor-Centric Policy 
Framework’. Vide our earlier order dated 27.10.2026, we had 
directed that a copy of the said Policy Framework be furnished 
to the learned Additional Solicitor General of India for 
examination by the Government of India, with a view to 
formulating a comprehensive pan-India policy. The Policy 
Framework also envisages a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) 
for the provision of first aid, along with a corresponding 
curriculum for schools and colleges. In this regard, we deem 
it appropriate to entrust NALSA with the responsibility of 
facilitating the coordination and dissemination of the 
aforesaid aspects of the Policy Framework, and in overseeing 
their progress and implementation. 
4.Further, we are constrained to express our concern that the 
easy and largely unregulated availability of acid in the open 
market continues to be a significant factor contributing to 
the menace of acid attacks. The directions issued by this 
Court on 18.07.2013 in Laxmi v. Union of India, W.P. (Crl.) 
No. 129/2006, were intended to address this concern precisely 
by regulating the sale and distribution of acid. However, as 
observed in our earlier order(s), these directions remain 
inadequately implemented. The unfortunate persistence of acid 
8

## Page 197

 
attacks is a stark reminder that the regulatory safeguards put 
in place by this Court have not achieved their intended 
purpose. 
5.In this backdrop, we deem it appropriate to impress upon the 
Union of India and the State Government(s) to consider the 
following measures, including through appropriate legislative 
or rule-making interventions, with a view to putting in place 
a comprehensive framework for regulating the sale of acid and 
preventing its misuse: 
i.Retail sale of acid by private persons, including through 
online or door-delivery platforms, be completely banned. 
ii.Retail sale of acid for medical purposes may be permitted 
only through medical stores or pharmacies attached to 
Government hospitals, and only upon obtaining the prior 
written approval of the Chief Medical Officer or the Civil 
Surgeon, as the case maybe. 
iii.Every such sale may be made against a prescribed Form 
recording the particulars of the buyer, including Aadhaar 
or any other Government-issued photo identity, the quantity 
and purpose of purchase, their address and contact details 
for easy identification. 
iv.The Form shall carry a declaration that the acid shall be 
used solely for the stated purpose, with the buyer being 
made liable, in accordance with law, for its diversion or 
misuse.  
v.The abovementioned diversion shall include misuse by any 
9

## Page 198

 
other person, whether with or without the knowledge of the 
buyer, making the buyer vicariously liable for such misuse. 
vi.The Form may further require particulars of the immovable 
property of the buyer, which may be attached, in accordance 
with law, in the event of misuse of the acid so purchased, 
for treatment and/or compensation of the victim(s). 
6.Pending formulation of such a policy, we deem it necessary to 
direct the Union of India, the States as well as the Union 
Territories to ensure strict enforcement of the directions in 
Laxmi (supra) and the Rules framed under the Poisons Act, 
1919. 
7.In compliance with our order dated 31.08.2026, the Petitioner 
has placed on record recommendations for the introduction of 
educational material on acid attack prevention, emergency 
response and the rights of survivors, in school and college 
curricula. It has been suggested that a model module be 
prepared by an Expert Committee, with all medical content 
developed or approved by qualified burn-care and emergency 
medicine professionals and without graphic imagery, comprising 
the following components:  
i.Prevention and responsible conduct, including consent, non-
violence, and recognizing stalking and harassment; 
ii.Emergency first aid and medical response, including calling 
112 and the ambulance, immediate and continuous irrigation 
with running water, and urgent hospital transfer; 
iii.Legal rights, hospital duties and access to legal aid and 
10

## Page 199

 
compensation; and 
iv.Rehabilitation, inclusion and survivor perspectives, 
including long-term medical and psychosocial needs and 
prevention of stigma. 
8.It is further suggested that the module be introduced in a 
phased, age-appropriate manner from middle school to higher 
education, through existing programmes on health, well-being 
and life-skills, in line with the National Curriculum 
Framework for School Education 2023 and as determined by 
NCERT. 
9.We find merit in these suggestions. Accordingly, we direct the 
Union of India, through the Ministry of Education and the 
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, to consider the 
desirability of constituting an Expert Committee, in 
consultation with the NCERT, the UGC, the National Medical 
Commission, National Legal Services Authority, the National 
Commission for Women, the State authorities, burn-care experts 
and survivor-led organisations, to develop the model module. 
10.The Union of India, in consultation with NALSA, is directed to 
determine the manner in which the proposed module as well as 
the SOP prepared by the Intervenor NGO is to be considered, 
developed, and implemented. NALSA, through its Member 
Secretary, is directed to coordinate with the concerned 
authorities and, at the appropriate stage, disseminate and 
monitor the module and the SOP, and undertake the necessary 
follow-up to ensure their effective implementation. In this 
11

## Page 200

 
regard, we deem it appropriate to further direct NALSA to 
submit periodic compliance reports every three months. 
11.Let the Union of India file an affidavit indicating the steps 
taken on the above within two weeks. Post the matter for 
further consideration on 14.12.2026. 
(ARJUN BISHT)                              (PREETHI DILEEP KUMAR) 
ASTT. REGISTRAR-cum-PS                        DY. REGISTRAR

O R D E R
1. This appeal, filed under Section 62 of the Insolvency and
Bankruptcy Code, 20161, arises out of the order dated 06.01.2025
passed by the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal2, Chennai,
in Company Appeal (AT)(CH)(INS) No. 439/2024.  On 27.01.2025,
while issuing notice in this appeal, this Court observed as
under: -
“It  is  submitted  that  during  the  course  of  a
Corporate  Insolvency  Resolution  Process,  when
proceedings for recovery are initiated, certain kinds
of ‘set-off’, such as equitable and contractual, are
permitted. The appellant, Embassy Commercial Projects
(Whitefield) Pvt. Ltd., would be entitled to raise
the contention of a ‘set-off’ during the arbitration
proceedings…….”
2. The issue, as aforestated, arises in the context of the
1  “IBC”, for short
2  “NCLAT”, for short
C.A. No. 942/2025     1

## Page 214

corporate insolvency resolution process initiated on 08.09.2023
against Katerra India Private Limited in CP(IB) No. 74/BB/2023
on the file of the National Company Law Tribunal3, Bengaluru
Bench at Bengaluru. Earlier thereto, the appellant, Embassy
Commercial Projects (Whitefield) Pvt. Ltd.4, was appointed as a
co-developer along with the corporate debtor to undertake the
development, operation and maintenance of a project. Prior to
initiation  of  the  corporate  insolvency  resolution  process
against the corporate debtor, on 31.01.2023, the appellant,
ECPPL, invoked the performance bank guarantees furnished to it
and informed the corporate debtor, by way of notice dated
03.04.2023, that it was still entitled to recover a sum of
77,17,46,138/- (Rupees seventy seven crore seventeen lakh₹
forty six thousand one hundred thirty eight), after adjustment
of  the  amounts  recovered  through  encashment  of  the  bank
guarantees. However, the corporate debtor issued reply notice
dated  11.07.2023,  wherein  it  claimed  that  a  sum  of
160,45,27,775/- (Rupees one hundred sixty crore forty five₹
lakh twenty seven thousand seven hundred and seventy five) was
due and payable to it.  
3. It was at this stage that the corporate debtor was subjected to
the corporate insolvency resolution process under the IBC.  The
appellant,  ECPPL,  submitted  its  claim  in  Form-F  under
Regulation 9A of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India
(Insolvency  Resolution  Process  for  Corporate  Persons)
3  “NCLT”, for short
4   “ECPPL”, for short
C.A. No. 942/2025     2

## Page 215

Regulations,  2016,  with  Pankaj  Srivastava,  the  Resolution
Professional (R.P.) of the corporate debtor, on 05.12.2023.  
4. In turn, Pankaj Srivastava, the R.P., issued a notice under
Section 21 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, to
the  appellant,  ECPPL,  and  the  principal  developer,  Vikas
Telecom Private Limited,  on 01.03.2024, seeking initiation of
arbitration  proceedings  as  per  the  contractual  clause.
Thereafter, by email dated 11.03.2024, Pankaj Srivastava, the
R.P., informed the appellant, ECPPL, that as its claim was
disputed and a claim of 160,45,27,775/- (Rupees one hundred₹
sixty crore forty five lakh twenty seven thousand seven hundred
seventy five) was raised against it, its claim was not being
admitted in the corporate insolvency resolution process.  
5. Thereupon, the appellant, ECPPL, filed I.A. No. 545/2024 in
CP(IB) No. 74/BB/2023 before the NCLT seeking a clarification
as to whether its claim stood extinguished under the approved
resolution plan.  This application was dismissed by the NCLT on
20.11.2024, taking note of the fact that the arbitration
proceedings had been initiated and the claim of the appellant,
ECPPL, was still indeterminate as on that date.
6. Aggrieved thereby, the appellant filed Company Appeal (AT)(CH)
(INS) No. 439/2024 before the NCLAT.  
7. This appeal was dismissed by way of the impugned judgment dated
06.01.2025.  The NCLAT opined that the appellant, ECPPL, was
attempting to get the decision that had already been taken by
Pankaj Srivastava, the R.P., on 11.03.2024, reconsidered, and
C.A. No. 942/2025     3

## Page 216

as the said decision had not been challenged independently and
had attained finality, it was not open to the appellant, ECPPL,
to raise the issue again.
8. At this stage, we may note that the corporate insolvency
resolution  process  culminated  in  a  ‘Successful  Resolution
Applicant’5 taking  over  the  corporate  debtor.  We  deem  it
appropriate to exercise power under Order I Rule 10(2) of the
Code of Civil Procedure, 19086, and add the SRA which has now
replaced the corporate debtor, that is, Nalwa Steel and Power
Limited7, P.B. No. 7, Gharghoda Road, Taraimal, Raigarh –
496001, Chhattisgarh, as respondent No.2.  Necessary amendment
shall be carried out in the cause title. In the light of the
SRA entering upon the scene, Pankaj Srivastava, the R.P.,
ceases to have any role to play.
9. The above facts demonstrate that, though the appellant, ECPPL,
attempted to seek a direction from the NCLT and thereafter, the
NCLAT, to the effect that its claim ought not to stand
extinguished under the approved resolution plan, that was not
the issue that was highlighted before this Court even at the
threshold. The only point that was raised was as to whether the
appellant, ECPPL, would have a right to claim a set-off in the
pending arbitration proceedings only to the extent of raising a
defence to the claim put forth on behalf of the corporate
debtor, which now stands substituted by NSPL, the SRA.
5   “SRA”, for short
6   “CPC”, for short
7   “NSPL”, for short
C.A. No. 942/2025     4

## Page 217

10. This issue stands squarely covered by the recent decisions of
this Court. We may note that this Court had occasion to deal
with a similar issue in  Bharti Airtel Limited & Anr. vs.
Vijaykumar V. Iyer & Ors.8  Therein, it was observed that a
statutory set-off in terms of Order VIII Rule 6 of the CPC or
an insolvency set-off, as permitted by Regulation 29 of the
Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (Liquidation Process)
Regulations, 2016, cannot be applied to corporate insolvency
resolution process. However, this Court added the caveat that
this would be subject to two exceptions – first, if at all it
could be called an exception, was where the party was entitled
to a contractual set-off, on the date which is effective before
or on the date the corporate insolvency resolution process was
put in motion; and the second exception was the case of an
‘equitable set-off’ when the claim and counter claim in the
form of set-off were linked and connected on account of one or
more transactions that could be treated as one. It was observed
that the set-off should be genuine and clearly established on
facts and in law, so as to make it inequitable and unfair that
the debtor be asked to pay money, without the adjustment
sought, that is fully justified and legal. It was further
observed  that  the  amount  to  be  adjusted  should  be  a
quantifiable and unquestionable monetary claim, as corporate
insolvency  resolution  process  is  a  time-bound  summary
procedure.  This Court, therefore, concluded that a set-off of
this nature should not require a legal proceeding and such set-
8   2024 INSC 15
C.A. No. 942/2025     5

## Page 218

off of money should be given against money only and would not
apply to assets.  Lastly, this Court opined that, as it was an
equitable right, it could be denied when grant of the relief
would defeat equity and justice.
11. More recently, in  Ujaas Energy Ltd. vs. West Bengal Power
Development Corporation Ltd.9, this Court was concerned with a
resolution plan which contained a clause that specifically
barred  payments  and  settlements  other  than  those  covered
thereby and categorically stated that no other payments or
settlements of any kind would have to be made to any other
person in respect of the claims of any person or Governmental
authority against the corporate debtor, whether or not filed or
admitted by the Resolution Professional, and all such claims
including counter claims in pending arbitration proceedings
would stand irrevocably and unconditionally abated, discharged,
settled and extinguished. Noting the aforestated clause in the
resolution plan, this Court observed that that the said clause
would not expressly, or even impliedly, exclude the plea of
set-off as a defence, as the same merely barred any claim for
the purpose of payment or settlement, and defensive use of the
claim of set-off had not been expressly covered. This Court,
accordingly, held that the respondent in that case would not be
entitled to independently pursue its claim by way of a counter
claim post the approval of the resolution plan, but it could be
permitted to raise plea of set-off, at least by way of defence.
Ordering so, this Court clarified as follows: -
9   2026 INSC 268
C.A. No. 942/2025     6

## Page 219

“27.  a. In the event the amount claimed in the
counterclaim of the respondent, or any part of it,
is found to be due and payable to the respondent by
the appellant and such amount exceeds the amount
awarded to the appellant, the surplus amount shall
not be recoverable by the respondent. 
b. Conversely, if any amount remains payable to the
appellant  after  adjustment  of  the  respondent’s
defence plea, the same shall be recoverable by the
appellant and the Tribunal may order accordingly. 
c. Further, if the arbitration proceedings initiated
by the appellant are withdrawn, the counterclaim of
the respondent shall also fail, as the same is
permitted only for the limited purpose of defence.”
12. Though the aforestated judgment ended with the observation that
it had been rendered considering the terms of a particular
paragraph of the resolution plan and was thus limited to the
facts and circumstances of that case, the principles culled out
as above are of guidance presently.
13. Thereafter,  in  Modern  Asset  vs.  KNK  Construction  Private
Limited10, this Court referred to Ujaas Energy Ltd. (supra) and
observed that, on facts, the appellant in that case also had a
right to raise the defence of set-off. It was opined that, just
as in the decision in Ujaas Energy Ltd. (supra), the appellant
should be permitted to raise a counter claim for the sole
purpose of claiming set-off but the appellant would not derive
any positive or affirmative relief of recovery on the basis of
that counter claim.  While disposing of the appeal, it was
10   2026 INSC 1103
C.A. No. 942/2025     7

## Page 220

affirmed that the appellant would be entitled to raise the
counter claim only for the purpose of set-off, and if any
amount was found due to be paid by the appellant to the
respondent, then there shall be set-off to the extent of the
entire counter claim, as put forth by the appellant. In the
extreme event of the claim of the respondent being found
untenable in toto, this Court observed that the appellant could
not seek any payment on the basis of such award since its claim
stood extinguished as against the corporate debtor and the SRA,
within the contours of the IBC.
14. In the light of the aforesaid settled legal position, the
learned senior counsel appearing for the appellant fairly
states that the appellant, ECPPL, would also seek identical
treatment in the pending arbitral proceedings initiated by the
corporate debtor, which now fall to the lot of NSPL, the SRA.  
15. We, therefore, make it clear that the appellant, ECPPL, on
grounds of equity and fairness, shall be entitled to raise the
defence of set-off only against the claim put forth by the
corporate debtor/SRA in the arbitral proceedings. In the event
of such claim being allowed and also the set-off claim by the
appellant,  ECPPL,  being  allowed,  the  appellant  would  be
entitled to adjust the amount claimed by it, by way of set-off.
In the event the corporate debtor/SRA fails to substantiate its
claim,  the  appellant,  ECPPL,  even  if  it  succeeds  in
establishing its counter claim, raised by way of a set-off,
would not be entitled to any payment.
C.A. No. 942/2025     8

## Page 221

16. Making this position clear, the appeal is allowed to the extent
indicated above.  Parties shall bear their own costs.
    Pending application(s) shall stand disposed of.
