4. In other words, it is the case of the appellant herein
that the period from the date of rejection or dismissal of the
reference till the period  of the Award being made afresh by
the Reference Court on restoration of the Reference Case (by
condonation  of  the  delay  in  filing  the  restoration
application) be excluded while computing the compensation
payable to the respondents/landowners under Section 28 of the
Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (for short, “the LA Act, 1894”).
5. We have heard Shri Kanakamedala Ravindra Kumar, learned
A.S.G. appearing for the appellant and Shri  Nachiketa Joshi,
learned  senior  counsel  appearing  for  the  respondents/
landowners and perused the material on record.
6. During the course of submission, it was contended by
learned A.S.G. that the Reference Court as well as the High
Court were not right in awarding statutory compensation @ 15%
per annum for the period, i.e., from the date of rejection of
the reference in the first instance till the date on which a
fresh Award was passed by the Reference Court. The reason
being, in the first instance the respondents/landowners did
not  take  steps  to  let  in  any  evidence  whatsoever.  The
Reference Court therefore, dismissed the reference as lacking
in evidence for seeking enhancement of compensation. It is
only  thereafter,  an  application  was  filed  for  seeking
restoration of the reference case on the file of the Reference
3

## Page 237

Court which was ordered by condoning the delay. Thereafter,
evidence was let in and Awards were made afresh but the
statutory interest under Section 28 of the LA Act, 1894 was
also awarded for the period referred to above.
7.  Learned A.S.G. submitted that when the landowners failed
to let in any evidence whatsoever before the Reference Court
in the first instance and did so only on restoration of their
reference, the landowners could not be benefited unjustly
owing to their own fault.  It was submitted that this Court
may modify the award by excluding statutory interest @ 15% per
annum being payable to the landowners/respondents herein from
the date on which their reference case was dismissed in the
first instance till the date on which the Awards were made
afresh on restoration of the reference case. He therefore,
submitted that while the appellant herein is not assailing the
quantum of compensation enhanced to the respondents herein,
they are only aggrieved by the award of statutory interest
under Section 28 of the LA Act, 1894 and hence the Awards may
be modified to that extent by also modifying the impugned
judgment of the High Court to that extent. 
8. Per contra, learned senior counsel Shri Joshi appearing
for the respondents/landowners vehemently contended that the
appellant herein ought not to have preferred these appeals
before this Court. No doubt, owing to the failure on the part
4

## Page 238

of the respondents in letting in evidence in the reference
cases,  these  cases  were  dismissed.  However,  restoration
applications filed by them were allowed on condoning the delay
in filing the same. Once the Reference Cases were restored,
evidence was let in and there was re-determination of the
compensation and enhanced compensation was awarded by the
Reference Court along with statutory interest under Section 28
of the LA Act, 1894. That the denial of the statutory interest
during the period when the matter was pending before the
Reference Court after restoration is not just and proper as
the pendency of the case before the Reference Court was not
owing to the fault of the landowners. He therefore, submitted
that there is no merit in these appeals and the same may be
dismissed.
9. In response to this submission, learned A.S.G contended
that the occasion to pass Awards afresh would not have arisen
at all had the respondents/landowners taken the opportunity to
let in evidence in the first instance. Not doing so, led to
the filing of the application seeking restoration for the
Reference Cases on the file of the Reference Court. Even after
restoration of the Reference cases, on many occasions, learned
counsel for the respondents/landowners did not appear. It was
dragged on for a long time and hence the appellant herein
cannot be saddled with a liability which was not owing to
5

## Page 239

their  fault  at  all  but  solely  on  account  of  the
procrastination of the cases by the respondents/landowners.
Therefore, he submitted that the exchequer cannot be burdened
with interest for the period during which the matter was
subsisting before the Reference Court solely owing to the
fault of the respondents/landowners.
10. We have considered the arguments advanced at the Bar and
perused the material on record.
11.  It  is  not  known  as  to  for  what  reason,  the
respondents/landowners who sought reference to the Reference
Court  under  Section  18  of  the  Act  for  enhancement  of
compensation failed to let in any evidence in the first
instance.  The fact however, remains that they did not let in
any  evidence  so  as  to  seek  enhanced  compensation.  The
Reference Court had no option except to dismiss the reference
owing to lack of evidence as the Land Acquisition Officer does
not have the onus to justify his Award. The burden lies on the
landowners to seek enhancement of compensation. The said
burden not having been discharged by the landowners, the
Reference  Court  rightly  dismissed  their  reference  cases.
However, subsequently, instead of filing appeals before the
High  Court,  the  landowners  sought  restoration  of  their
reference cases by seeking condonation of delay in filing the
said application. The Reference Court in its discretion has
6

## Page 240

not  only  condoned  the  delay  in  filing  the  restoration
application  but  later  has  also  allowed  the  restoration
application and has re-determined the enhanced compensation on
the basis of the evidence let in.  This is a case where the
respondents/landowners have had two opportunities to let in
evidence. No reason whatsoever or explanation has been offered
as to why they could not let in evidence in the first
instance. For not letting in any evidence, the Reference Court
dismissed their reference cases.  As we have noted, thereafter
another opportunity was given to them to let in evidence and
the enhanced compensation has been awarded. But for the period
from the date of rejection of the reference till the date on
which the enhanced compensation was awarded, learned A.S.G.
submitted that no statutory interest could be payable.  This
is  because  of  the  default  and  delay  caused  by  the
respondents/landowners.
12. We find force in the arguments of the learned A.S.G. In
the circumstances, we accept the said contention and we hold
that for the period from the date of rejection of reference
till the date of passing of the Awards afresh, no statutory
interest under Section 28 of the LA Act, 1894 shall be
payable.  But  for  the  period  prior  thereto  and  for  the
subsequent period, such interest shall be payable. 
13. We, therefore, clarify that for the period earlier to the
7

## Page 241

rejection of the Reference and for the period after the
enhancement  of  compensation  by  the  Reference  Court,  the
statutory interest under Section 28 of the LA Act, 1894 shall
be payable. 
14. Learned  A.S.G.  at  this  stage  submitted  that  the
compensation amount has been deposited before the Reference
Court.  The Reference Court shall re-compute the amount
payable to the respondents/landowners and permit them to
withdraw the same.
The appeals are allowed in part in the aforesaid terms. 
No costs.

of the opinion that the husband and wife both being young, should
amicably settle their differences or peacefully agree to part ways,
and hence directed mediation. However, after repeated mediation,
the parties have not been able to settle. From the orders passed, it
is very evident that the husband was ready for settlement, but the
wife refused to relent. 
4. We extract order dated 17.09.2026 as under:
‘1. In the transfer petition filed by the wife, we directed
both  parties  to  go  for  mediation,  considering  the  short
marital  life  they  had  and  their  young  age.  However,
mediation has failed and even though we had directed the
parties to make a further attempt and also directed the
husband,  respondent  herein  to  make  a  deposit  of
Rs.6,00,000/-, which was permitted to be withdrawn by the
petitioner-wife, no resolution has been arrived at.

## Page 246

3
2. However  today,  Ms.  Uttara  Babbar,  learned  Senior
Counsel appearing for the petitioner-wife and Mr. Shadan
Farasat,  learned  Senior  Counsel  appearing  for  the
respondent-husband submits that despite best efforts, they
have not been able to settle the matter, even  with the
active intervention of the learned Senior Counsel appearing
for both parties. 
3. Mr.  Shadan  Farasat  submits  that  since  exorbitant
sums were claimed by the petitioner-wife, no settlement
could  be  reached  and  the  respondent-husband  is  also
concerned with the maintenance granted of Rs.1 lakh per
month, which is challenged in the connected SLP. 
4. We  notice  that  the  marriage  was  solemnized  on
16.02.2021 and they were separated on 27.04.2022, within
which period  their  cohabitation was limited to a  month,
immediately after which the respondent left for the USA
and  later  from  03.12.2021 when  the petitioner-wife  was
taken to the USA. After she returned to attend her sister's
marriage, she has not gone back to join her husband. There
are no children born from the wedlock.
5. In the above circumstances, we are of the opinion that
the marriage is irretrievably broken down and there is no
point in the parties fighting over trivial issues, which could
put their future lives into jeopardy. 
6. In the above circumstances, we are of the opinion that
as permanent alimony the respondent-husband should pay
an amount of Rs.90,00,000/- in full and final settlement of
claims  raised  by  the  petitioner-wife  with  respect  to  the
marriage.  Learned  Senior  Counsel  appearing  for  the
petitioner-wife  submits  that  the  wife’s  jewellery,  she
received from her family at the time of marriage is still with
the respondent-husband. Learned Senior Counsel for the
respondent-husband submits that as per his instructions,
the petitioner-wife had taken the entire jewellery, when she
left the matrimonial home and if at all there is anything
remaining, it will be handed over within four weeks. 
7. We, hence direct the alimony fixed by us to be paid
within  four  weeks  from  today  and  if  any  jewellery  is
remaining with the respondent-husband the same shall also
be returned. If the petitioner-wife refuses to give the bank

## Page 247

4
details to facilitate the transfer of funds, the respondent-
husband shall be ready with a Demand Draft in the name of
the petitioner- wife on the next date of hearing. The matter
shall be posted after four weeks and in the meanwhile, we
direct that all proceedings between the parties with respect
to the marriage, both civil and criminal, shall stand stayed.
Order of maintenance also shall remain stayed till further
orders. On satisfaction of the amounts directed by us, the
respondent-husband would be entitled to file an application
invoking  Article  142  of  the  Constitution  of  India  for
dissolution  of  the  marriage  on  grounds  of  irretrievable
breakdown. 
8. Post the matter on 28.10.2026.’
5. Heard Sri Amit Rawal, learned Senior Counsel for the petitioner-
wife  and  Sri  Shadan  Farasat,  learned  Senior  Counsel  for  the
respondent-husband in the Transfer Petition and vice versa in the
Criminal Appeals.
6. Sri Shadan Farasat submits that the entire amounts, as directed
in  the earlier  order,  has  been  paid  to  the  wife.  Sri  Amit Rawal,
however, submits that the wife has accepted the money without
prejudice and she had never consented to the earlier order passed.
Admittedly, there was another learned Senior Counsel appearing for
the wife at the earlier point of time before this very same Bench. We
do  not  recall  the  learned  Senior  Counsel  appearing  for  the  wife
having, at all, consented to the order. She fairly submitted the views
of the wife and left it at that. The order passed by us on 17.09.2026
extracted hereinabove also does not record any consent. We were of

## Page 248

5
the opinion that there should be quietus to the issue and hence, the
said order. 
7. At this point, the wife who was present-in-person along with her
mother, interjected and poured her heart out regarding the marriage
and  the  ill-treatment  meted  out.  She  also  submitted  that  the
marriage was solemnized only on the undertaking of the husband
that he would continue in India. It is submitted that she had given up
her job and there is no possibility of a second marriage and she
insists on the continuance of maintenance, as awarded by the High
Court. She also expressed her inability to concede or consent to
divorce. 
8. Sri  Amit  Rawal  pointed  out  that  there  are  some  items  of
stridhan, together with 16 coins of silver, which the wife had left at
the  husband’s  house.  It  is  contented  that  her  passport  and  her
educational certificates were with the husband’s family. Sri Shadan
Farasat fairly submitted that despite the husband not having located
the 16 silver coins, to bring a quietus to the issue, he has minted
newly ones, and he is ready to hand over the same to the wife or her
Counsel. As far as the certificates are concerned, the father-in-law
who was present in person, submits that there are no certificates or
passport  available  with  the  family  of  the  husband.  It  is  also
submitted by Sri Shadan Farasat that definitely the passport and

## Page 249

6
certificates could be applied for and obtained without any difficulty
and the contention made of the same being in the custody of the
husband is only to prolong and protract the matter.
9. Having  heard  the  parties  and  keeping  in  mind  the  earlier
proceedings,  we  are  of  the  opinion  that  the  marriage  has
irretrievably broken down. An application is filed by the husband
invoking Article 142 of the Constitution of India. We have already
noticed that the wife does not agree to the same but, however, we
do  not  see  any  other  feasible  option,  and  in  any  event,  the
arguments addressed on both sides indicate a complete breakdown
of marriage, which has no chance of being retrieved. The husband
had deposited a sum of Rs.6,00,000/- before the Registry, which was
disbursed to the wife, and later, on our orders, Rs.90,00,000/- has
been sent to the wife against the offer made by the husband as
recorded  in  our  order  dated  17.09.2025  of  Rs.35,00,000/-  to
Rs.40,00,000/- for an amicable settlement. 
10. We are convinced that the wife has fairly been compensated for
the  travails,  if  any,  she  had  to  undergo.  We,  hence,  invoke  the
extraordinary powers under Article 142 of the Constitution of India to
dissolve the marriage between the parties. Decree  of  divorce  be
drawn accordingly.
11. In the context of the settlement made, we also set aside the

## Page 250

7
order of the High Court in the appeals filed against the common
order in the two revisions. The revision filed by the husband would
stand allowed and that filed by the wife would stand dismissed.
Needless to say, that the order of the Family Court shall also stand
reversed  and  the  proceedings  before  the  Family  Court  for
maintenance stand closed. 
12. We also make it clear that any other civil or criminal cases
pending between the parties shall not be proceeded with. Either of
the parties would be entitled to produce this order before the Court
where such proceeding is pending, to bring quietus to the matter.
13. The Transfer Petition is disposed of. 
14. The Appeals are disposed of in the above terms.
15. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.

as were available to parcel porters who had

present  applicants  (i.e.  the  respondents
herein) were engaged as licensed porters in
2011 and in 2014 identity cards qua their
functioning  as  parcel  porters  were
unauthorizedly issued, and taking advantage
of those cards O.A. was filed immediately in
the year 2015. In such circumstances, the
original  applicants  herein  cannot  be
considered similarly circumstanced as those
who were granted relief by CAT in respect of
their  functioning  as  parcel  porters  at
railway stations Bhagalpur, Sahibganj, and
Jamalpur. It has also been submitted that
there is no discussion in the judgment of
4

## Page 266

either CAT or the High Court whether any
circular  or  rule  entitles  the  original
applicants  to  regularization  of  their
service.  In  such  circumstances,  it  is
submitted,  the  order  of  CAT  requires
interference, CAT must reconsider the case.
10. Per  contra,  on  behalf  of  the
respondents, it is submitted that there is
no dispute that the original applicants were
issued identity cards for their working as
parcel porters. Further, there is no serious
dispute  of  their  functioning  as  parcel
porters. Besides, their license as porters
were not renewed. Therefore, if work was
being taken from them under the identity
cards held by them, it could safely be
inferred that they had been performing their
duties under the Railway administration as
parcel porters and were, therefore, entitled
to the benefit of absorption as was accorded
to  parcel  porters  functioning  at  other
Railway stations.
11. We have accorded due consideration to
5

## Page 267

the rival contentions and have perused the
materials brought on record.
12. What is important to note is that CAT
has granted relief to the respondents not by
placing  reliance  on  any  service  rules
regulations,  notifications,  circulars  or
memorandums but on the ground that they were
similarly circumstanced as those who were
granted benefit under the orders of CAT
passed earlier in respect of parcel porters
functioning at Railway stations Bhagalpur,
Sahibganj,  and  Jamalpur  under  the  Malda
Division.
13. A perusal of the order passed on the
petition of parcel porters engaged at those
Railway stations would indicate that they
had  claimed  to  be  serving  the  Railway
administration  since  1974.  Their  claim
petition  was  filed  in  1997.  In  such
circumstances, they had served the Railway
administration for over two decades. The
original applicants herein on the other hand
had not even served for a decade. Therefore,
6

## Page 268

the view taken by CAT that the original
applicants  herein  were  similarly
circumstanced  as  those  who  were  granted
relief earlier by CAT is not sustainable. In
case the original applicants were otherwise
entitled for the benefit sought by them in
their  original  application  needs  to  be
considered based on other materials that may
be available on record. However, since CAT
has not taken notice of any other material
which may entitle the original applicants
for absorption /regularization, the matter
would require reconsideration. Importantly,
the only material which has been accorded
consideration for granting relief to the
original applicants is the earlier judgment
of  CAT  which,  in  our  view,  is
distinguishable on the facts of the present
case.
14. We are, therefore, of the view that
CAT  needs  to  reconsider  the  matter  in
accordance with law.
15. Accordingly, we deem it appropriate to
7

## Page 269

allow this appeal and remit the matter to
CAT for a fresh consideration.
16. The appeal is, accordingly, allowed.
The impugned order of the High Court as well
as CAT is set aside. Original Application
No. 350/1517/2015 shall stand restored on
the file of CAT, Kolkata Bench, Kolkata and
shall be decided afresh in accordance with
law after giving opportunity of hearing to
the parties.
17. As the Original Application is of the
year 2015, we deem it appropriate to direct
CAT to ensure that the same is decided
expeditiously preferably within a period of
nine months.
18. Pending application(s), if any, shall
stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.        OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP (Civil) No. 22930 of 2026)
KISLAY THAKUR APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
UNION OF INDIA & ORS.    RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The appellant before this Court has filed the
present appeal being aggrieved by the impugned
judgment and order dated 10.03.2026 passed by the
High Court of Delhi at New Delhi in W.P. (C) No.
18276 of 2025.
3. The  facts  of  the  case  reveal  that  the
appellant, pursuant to an advertisement, applied
for the post of Constable (GD) in the Central Armed
Police Forces and was duly selected. However, on
account of a criminal case which had resulted in
his acquittal, he was not issued an appointment
1

## Page 290

order. The writ petition preferred by the appellant
before the High Court of Delhi claiming appointment
was also dismissed.
4. Learned counsel appearing for the appellant
has stated before this Court that the criminal
dispute was between the appellant and his family
members, and later on, the same resulted in his
acquittal.
5. Though  the  learned  Additional  Solicitor
General  appearing  for  the  respondent(s)  has
vehemently  argued  that  the  acquittal  was  on
technical grounds and cannot be treated as a clean
acquittal, this Court, in a similar case involving
almost  identical  facts  and  circumstances,  has
decided SLP (C) Nos. 3419–3421 of 2026 (Union of
India  &  Anr.  vs.  Srikanta  Gorain  &  Ors.).
Paragraphs  4  to  8  of  the  said  judgment  are
reproduced as under:
“4. For the purpose of guidance of the
appointing authorities, we propose to
emphasize that while dealing with cases
of the present nature, the appointing
authority ought not to get unduly swayed
merely because of user of the expression
2

## Page 291

“benefit of doubt” by the trial court in
its  judgment.  An  acquittal  could  be
based on technicality or upon a full
consideration of the prosecution case.
The  judgment  of  acquittal  in  its
entirety has to be read to ascertain
whether  the  acquittal  that  has  been
recorded is other than honourable. If
witnesses do not turn up for tendering
evidence  or  turn  hostile  or  the
investigation is found to be flawed or
there  be  any  such  similar  vitiating
factor and if these give rise to a
lingering suspicion in the mind of the
trial court that the witnesses have been
won  over  or  that  the  evidence  has
deliberately been withheld but, at the
same  time,  the  evidence/materials  on
record  are  absolutely  inadequate  or
insufficient  to  record  a  finding  of
guilt, the trial courts are generally
prone to record acquittal of the accused
by giving them the benefit of doubt.
Such  an  acquittal  being  based  on
technical  grounds  or  on  “benefit  of
doubt” would obviously fall short of an
honourable acquittal. But, if the trial
court upon consideration of the entirety
of the evidence on record finds that the
charge  has  not  been  proved  beyond
reasonable  doubt,  yet,  acquits  the
accused by recording that he is given
the  benefit  of  doubt,  a  claim  of
honourable acquittal could certainly be
raised notwithstanding such recording.
After  all,  the  onus  is  on  the
prosecution to prove the guilt of the
3

## Page 292

accused  beyond  all  reasonable  doubt.
Much would, therefore, depend on witness
behaviour  and  how  the  trial  court
appreciates and analyses the evidence.
More often than not, it is found that
the trial courts after recording that
the prosecution has miserably failed to
prove its case follows it up by giving
the accused the “benefit of doubt”. If
such be the finding, i.e., the accused
is exonerated with no suspicion left, it
would be thoroughly improper, unfair and
unjust to deny an appointment on the
specious ground of the acquittal being
based on what the trial court terms as
“benefit of doubt”.
5. Doubtless, the appointing authorities
are the sole judges of eligibility and
suitability of any individual aspiring
for  an  appointment  in  a  disciplined
force.  It  is  equally  true  that  the
appointing  authorities  do  have  an
onerous duty of selecting individuals
who have clean antecedents. However, the
power  to  scrutinize  claims  for
appointments  and  to  proceed  in  that
direction requires exercise of due care,
caution and circumspection. The power
cannot be exercised arbitrarily to the
detriment and prejudice of prospective
appointees by rejecting their claims,
despite  their  fulfilment  of  other
criteria, for no better reason than that
such appointee had figured as an accused
in a crime. The decision not to appoint
must be based on sound reasons evincing
application  of  mind  to  all  relevant
4

## Page 293

factors or else the same would be liable
to judicial interdiction.
6. Although  in  a  slightly  different
context, in State of Madhya Pradesh v.
Ramashanker  Raghuvanshi,  this  Court
posed the question : whether Government
service is a heaven where only angels
can  seek  entry?  This  decision  was
noticed  in  subsequent  decisions  too,
viz. K. Vijaya Lakshmi v. State of A.P.
and Avtar Singh v. Union of India. We
can take judicial notice that over the
past several years, across the country,
quite a few of the incidents giving rise
to registration of crimes are either
politically  motivated  or  designed  to
deprive someone of his legitimate dues.
Unless there are strong reasons to hold
the view that a prospective appointee
has  indulged  in  serious  criminal  or
other  subversive  activity  thereby
disentitling him to an appointment, he
may not be denied such appointment on
hyper-technical  grounds  in  these
challenging times of lack of adequate
opportunity of public employment.
7. What has also not escaped our notice
is that the respondents 1, 2 and 3 did
not attempt to secure public employment
by  deception.  They  were  honest  and
truthful  in  their  versions,  a  fact
admitted even by Mr. Sanjay. As such,
the  restrictions  envisaged  in  the
relevant  circulars  applicable  to  the
CISF could not have been invoked in any
of the three cases under consideration
to deny the benefits of appointment to
5

## Page 294

the respondents 1, 2 and 3.
8. Since the impugned judgment and order
of the Delhi High Court is based on
proper  appreciation  of  the  relevant
circulars as well as on a correct and
proper  understanding  of  the  reasons
assigned by the respective trial courts
while acquitting the respondents 1, 2
and 3, we see no reason to interfere
therewith;  hence,  the  special  leave
petitions are dismissed.”
6. In light of the aforesaid judgment delivered
by a Coordinate Bench of this Court, the impugned
judgment and order dated 10.03.2026 passed by the
High Court of Delhi in W.P. (C) No. 18276 of 2025
is set aside.
7. The respondent(s) is directed to issue an
appointment order in favour of the appellant within
a  period  of  30  days  from  today.  To  be  more
specific,  the  appellant  shall  be  entitled  to
seniority as per the select/merit list from the
date  other  candidates  were  granted  appointment
pursuant to the same selection process, along with
other consequential benefits, however, he shall not
be entitled to any back wages/financial benefits
6

## Page 295

for the past period.
8. With the aforesaid observations, the appeal
stands allowed.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

3. Owing to matrimonial discord, the petitioner-wife was 
allegedly compelled to leave her matrimonial home on 
6th August, 2023. 
4. In September 2024, the petitioner-wife instituted 
Matrimonial Case No. 543 of 2024 under Section 9 of 

## Page 307

T.P.(C) NO.2605/2025  2 
 
the HMA before the Family Court, Muzaffarpur, Bihar, 
seeking restitution of conjugal rights. 
5. Subsequently, the respondent-husband instituted HMA 
No. 1561 of 2024 under Section 13(1)(ia) of the HMA 
before the Family Court, Gurugram, Haryana, seeking 
dissolution of marriage on the ground of cruelty. The 
summons in the said proceedings were received by the 
petitioner-wife on 7th January, 2025. 
6. It is the aforesaid proceedings instituted by the 
respondent-husband that the petitioner-wife seeks to 
have transferred, giving rise to the present transfer 
petition. 
7. By order dated 6th May, 2026, this Court referred the 
disputes between the parties to the Supreme Court 
Mediation Centre to explore the possibility of an 
amicable resolution. Pursuant thereto, the parties 
entered into a Settlement Agreement dated 27th May, 
2026, whereby they amicably resolved their 
matrimonial disputes. 
8. The parties have jointly filed I.A. No. 267415 of 2026 
under Article 142 of the Constitution of India, seeking 
appropriate orders in terms of the Settlement 
Agreement, including dissolution of their marriage by 
mutual consent and closure of the pending proceedings 
between them. 
9. We have perused the Settlement Agreement and 
interacted with the parties, who have appeared before 
us through video conferencing. Both parties have 

## Page 308

T.P.(C) NO.2605/2025  3 
 
affirmed that the settlement has been arrived at 
voluntarily, of their own free will, and without any 
coercion, duress, undue influence, fraud or collusion. 
They have further affirmed that all disputes and 
differences arising out of their matrimonial relationship 
have been amicably resolved, that no claims or 
demands remain outstanding between them, and that 
there is no possibility of reconciliation. 
10. The material terms of the Settlement Agreement, as 
recorded in I.A. No. 267415 of 2026, are reproduced 
hereinbelow: - 
“6. That the salient terms of the Settlement 
Agreement dated 27th May, 2026, inter alia, 
are as under: 
 
(a) The parties have confirmed and declared 
that there is no possibility of re-union and 
that they have voluntarily and of their 
own free will decided to dissolve their 
marriage by mutual consent; 
 
(b) Neither party shall pay any amount, 
money, compensation, maintenance, 
alimony, settlement amount or any other 
monetary sum to the other in any manner 
whatsoever, and all claims of either party, 
whether past, present or future, including 
claims relating to maintenance, 
permanent alimony, stridhan, jewellery, 
articles, expenses, compensation or any 
other monetary or non-monetary claim, 
stand fully and finally settled without any 
payment by either party to the other, save 
and except the personal belongings of the 
Petitioner contained in one trunk lying at 
the residence of the Respondent at 
Muzaffarpur along with the engagement 
ring of the Petitioner, which were to be 

## Page 309

T.P.(C) NO.2605/2025  4 
 
handed over to the father of the Petitioner 
on or before 05.06.2026; 
(c) The parties have agreed to jointly pray to 
this Hon'ble Court to exercise its powers 
under Article 142 of the Constitution of 
India and grant a decree of divorce by 
mutual consent, and to jointly pray for 
closure, quashing, withdrawal and/or 
disposal of all cases, complaints, 
proceedings and disputes between them, 
whether criminal or civil; 
(d) The Confirming Party has confirmed that 
Criminal Complaint bearing No. Cr. Cases 
Complaint (P) 2530/2023 arose out of the 
matrimonial dispute between the parties, 
has no objection to its closure, 
withdrawal, quashing and/or disposal, 
and has undertaken not to pursue the 
said complaint any further against th 
Petitioner or her family members; 
(e) All pending cases, complaints, 
proceedings, revisions, appeals or claims 
arising out of the matrimonial 
relationship and/or the disputes between 
the parties, whether specifically 
mentioned in the Settlement Agreement 
or not, shall be withdrawn, closed, 
quashed and/or disposed of in terms of 
the Settlement Agreement, and the 
parties have further undertaken not to 
initiate any fresh litigation, complaint or 
proceeding against each other or against 
their respective family members in 
relation to the present matrimonial 
dispute. 
… 
8. That in due compliance of the Settlement 
Agreement dated 27.05.2026, the personal 
belongings of the Petitioner contained in one 
trunk, along with the engagement ring of the 
Petitioner, have been handed over to the 
father of the Petitioner on 04.06.2026. 
Nothing further remains to be performed by 
either party under the Settlement Agreement, 
save and except the reliefs prayed for.” 

## Page 310

T.P.(C) NO.2605/2025  5 
 
 
11. We have considered the Settlement Agreement dated 
27th May, 2026, the joint application filed by the parties 
and the statements made before us. The parties have 
confirmed that the personal belongings of the 
petitioner-wife, including the engagement ring, have 
already been handed over to her father on 4th June, 
2026. It has also been affirmed that nothing further 
remains to be performed under the settlement, save and 
except the reliefs sought before this Court. 
12. Having regard to the fact that the parties have been 
living separately for more than three years, that all 
disputes arising out of their matrimonial relationship 
have been amicably resolved, that the settlement has 
been arrived at voluntarily and without coercion, and 
that there is no possibility of reconciliation, we are 
satisfied that the settlement is genuine, voluntary and 
bona fide and deserves to be given effect to. 
13. We place on record our appreciation for the 
commendable efforts of Mr. Neeraj Dutt Gaur, Mr. 
Rajesh Dham, Ms. Geetanjali Sahni Atri and Mr. Vikas 
Bali, learned Mediators at the Supreme Court Mediation 
Centre, whose sincere and effective efforts facilitated 
the amicable resolution of the disputes between the 
parties. 
14. In view of the aforesaid circumstances, we are of the 
considered view that the present case is a fit case for 
exercise of the jurisdiction of this Court under Article 

## Page 311

T.P.(C) NO.2605/2025  6 
 
142 of the Constitution of India, so as to bring a quietus 
to the disputes between the parties and secure complete 
justice. 
15. Accordingly, I.A. No. 267415 of 2026 is allowed in terms 
of the Settlement Agreement dated 27th May, 2026. In 
exercise of our powers under Article 142 of the 
Constitution of India, we issue the following directions: 
- 
i. The marriage solemnized between the petitioner-
wife and the respondent-husband on 25th January, 
2023 is hereby dissolved by a decree of divorce by 
mutual consent. 
ii. The following cases/proceedings pending between 
the parties and arising out of their matrimonial 
relationship shall stand quashed and closed: - 
a) Maintenance Case No. 276/2024 titled “Neha 
Kumari v. Vishal Kumar Singh”, filed by the 
Petitioner under Section 144 of the Bharatiya 
Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, pending 
before the Ld. Principal Judge, Family Court, 
Muzaffarpur, Bihar; 
b) Matrimonial Case No. 543/2024 titled “Neha 
Kumari v. Vishal Kumar Singh”, filed by the 
Petitioner under Section 9 of the Hindu Marriage 
Act, 1955, pending before the Ld. Principal 
Judge, Family Court, Muzaffarpur, Bihar. 
c) HMA Petition No. 1561/2024 titled “Vishal 
Kumar Singh v. Neha Singh”, filed by the 

## Page 312

T.P.(C) NO.2605/2025  7 
 
Respondent under Section 13(1)(ia) of the Hindu 
Marriage Act, 1955, pending before the Ld. 
Additional Principal Judge, Family Court, 
Gurugram, Haryana; 
d) Criminal Complaint bearing No. Cr. Cases 
Complaint (P) 2530/2023 titled “Ajit Kumar v. 
Neha Kumari & Ors.”, filed by Mr. Ajit Kumar, 
brother of the Respondent, against the 
Petitioner, Shri Sunil Kumar Singh and Smt. 
Babita Singh, pending before the Court of the 
Ld. Judicial Magistrate 1st Class, East,

e) Complaint Case No. 3591/2024 filed by the

S.D.J.M., East, Muzaffarpur, Bihar, which came 
to be dismissed vide order dated 17.07.2025 and 
which stands revived pursuant to the order 
dated 22.05.2026 passed in Criminal Revision 
No. 250/2025 filed by the Petitioner. 
iii. The aforesaid list is illustrative and not exhaustive. 
Any other case, complaint, proceeding, petition, 
suit or litigation, whether civil or criminal, pending 
between the parties and arising out of or in 
connection with their matrimonial relationship or 
the disputes and differences settled under the 
Settlement Agreement dated 20th August, 2026, 
shall also stand quashed, withdrawn and/or 
closed, as the case may be. 

## Page 313

iv. The parties shall not hereafter initiate, institute or 
pursue any fresh complaint, proceeding, petition,

Mr. Davinder Pal Singh, learned Additional Solicitor General, and
Ms. Vidhi Gupta, learned counsel appearing for the CBI and Mr. B.
Karunakaran, learned counsel appearing for the respondent(s).
2. The present batch of Special Leave Petitions has been filed at
the instance of the accused, namely, Aswathaman (A-3), Pradeep (A-
16), Hariharan (A-17), Sathishkumar (A-20), Siva (A-21), Appu @
Pudhur Appu (A-22), Mukilan (A-23), Noor @ Vijay @ Vijayakumar (A-
24), Vignesh @ Appu (A-25), Rajesh (A-26), Gopi (A-27) and Kumara @
Senthilkumar (A-28), calling in question the common order passed by
the High Court of judicature at Madras, whereby the orders granting
bail to them by the Trial Court on different dates were set aside.
3. The First Information Report (FIR) in respect of the murder of

## Page 317

4
one Armstrong came to be registered on 05.07.2024, being Crime No.
293/2024, at K-1 Sembium Police Station, Chennai. Upon completion
of the investigation, the State Police filed a chargesheet on
03.10.2024 against 30 accused persons for offences punishable under
Sections 191(2), 191(3), 118(1) read with Sections 103(1), 109,
190, 351(3) read with Section 61(2)(a), 49 and 238 of the Bharatiya
Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Section 4(b) read with Sections 5 and 6 of the
Explosive Substances Act, 1908, and Section 3 read with Section
25(1B)(a) of the Arms Act, 1959.
4. The brother of the deceased, namely, K. Immanuvel @ Keynos
Armstrong, filed a Criminal Original Petition bearing Crl.O.P. No.
18671 of 2025 before the High Court of Judicature at Madras,
seeking transfer of the investigation in Crime No. 293/2024 to the
Central Bureau of Investigation (for short, ‘CBI’).
5. On 24.09.2025, the High Court, while quashing the chargesheet
filed by the State Police, directed transfer of the investigation
to the CBI.
6. Aggrieved by the aforesaid order, the State of Tamil Nadu
approached this Court by filing SLP (Crl.) No. 15897/2025. This
Court, by its order dated 10.10.2025, stayed the order of the High
Court insofar as it quashed the chargesheet filed by the State
Police was concerned, while permitting the direction for transfer
of investigation to the CBI to remain operative.
7. In the meantime, between 13.10.2025 and 10.11.2025, the twelve
petitioners before us were granted bail by the Trial Court on

## Page 318

5
different dates.
8. Subsequently, on 27.02.2026, on the applications moved by the
wife of the deceased, Porkodi, the High Court set aside the orders
granting bail to the aforesaid twelve accused persons.
9. It is pertinent to note that, on 22.07.2026, SLP (Crl.) No.
15897/2025, filed by the State of Tamil Nadu, came to be dismissed
as withdrawn. Consequently, the order dated 24.09.2025 passed by
the High Court, directing transfer of the investigation to the CBI,
became operative, and the CBI continued as the investigating agency
in the matter.
10. Upon transfer of the investigation, the CBI re-registered the
FIR on 06.08.2026 as RC No. RC9/5/2026/CBI/CTB/Chennai.
11. On this Court being moved by the aggrieved accused against the
order dated 27.02.2026 setting aside their bail, this Court, vide
order dated 12.03.2026, continued the interim protection granted to
the petitioners by extending the stay of cancellation of their bail
on the same terms and conditions as imposed by the Trial Court.
12. When the matter was taken up today, Mr. Davinder Pal Singh,
learned Additional Solicitor General, with his usual fairness,
submitted that, insofar as A-23, Mukilan; A-24, Noor @ Vijay @
Vijayakumar; A-25, Vignesh @ Appu; A-27, Gopi; A-28, Kumara @
Senthilkumar; A-16, Pradeep; and A-20, Sathishkumar, are concerned,
the CBI does not press for setting aside the orders granting bail
to them.
13.  The aforesaid statement is taken on record.

## Page 319

6
14. In view of the statement made by the learned Additional
Solicitor General, the Special Leave Petitions, insofar as the
aforesaid  seven  accused  persons  are  concerned,  are  allowed.
Consequently, the impugned order, insofar as it sets aside the
orders granting bail to the aforesaid seven accused persons, is set
aside.
15. Mr. Davinder Pal Singh, learned Additional Solicitor General,
further submits that, insofar as A-3, Aswathaman; A-21, Siva; A-22,
Appu  @  Pudhur  Appu;  A-26,  Rajesh;  and  A-17,  Hariharan  are
concerned, the CBI is desirous of placing certain aspects before
the Court to support the order setting aside the bail granted to
the said accused persons.
16. Mr. Davinder Pal Singh, learned Additional Solicitor General,
also points out that, insofar as ten other accused persons, who are
not  petitioners  before  this  Court  in  the  present  batch  of
proceedings,  are  concerned,  the  CBI  has  already  initiated
proceedings before the High Court seeking cancellation of their
bail. The said proceedings are pending in Crl.O.P. Nos. 77333,
77337 and 77335 of 2026.
17.  Having regard to the submissions advanced on behalf of the
CBI, we are of the opinion that, instead of this Court examining
the aspects which the CBI seeks to highlight in respect of A-3,
Aswathaman; A-21, Siva; A-22, Appu @ Pudhur Appu; A-26, Rajesh; and
A-17, Hariharan, the High Court should have the first opportunity
to examine the same.

## Page 320

7
18. Accordingly, the impugned order is set aside qua the said five
accused also. However, the proceedings concerning the aforesaid
five accused persons are remitted to the High Court for fresh
consideration. It is directed that the aforesaid five accused
persons shall continue to remain on bail on the same terms and
conditions as imposed by the Trial Court, during the pendency of
the proceedings before the High Court.
19. We also find merit in the submission made by the learned
Additional Solicitor General that the Criminal Original Petitions
so remitted to the High Court should be heard along with the
Criminal Original Petitions filed by the CBI seeking cancellation
of bail granted to the ten other accused persons who are not
petitioners before this Court.
20. The Special Leave Petitions stand disposed of in the above
terms.
21. Needless to observe that the High Court shall consider the
matter independently uninfluenced by any of the observations made
either in the present order or in the impugned order passed by the
High Court.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. By an order dated 25.08.2022, a Two-Judge Bench has
referred this matter to a larger Bench for consideration
of the question mentioned therein. The said order is
reproduced hereasunder:-
“Leave granted. 
Learned  counsel  for  the  insurance
company  relies  upon  two  judgments  of  this
Court reported as 2006 (4) SCC 404 and 2008
(7) SCC 428 to contend that a pillion rider on
a motorcycle is not a third party, therefore,
the  insurance  company  is  not  liable  to
5

## Page 327

indemnify  the  insured  on  account  of  the
injuries or death of such pillion rider. 
The  basis  of  the  said  argument  is
Indian Motor Tariff Endorsement No. 70, which
is to the effect that in “Act Only” policy,
the insured has to pay extra premium to cover
the pillion rider. 
However, the question as to whether the
third party includes all other persons other
than the insured, who is the first party and
the  insurer,  who  is  the  second  party.
Therefore, all other persons who are neither
the insured nor the insurer will be third
party and will be covered by the Act Only
policy, we have prima facie reservation about
the view expressed. Such question is required
to be determined authoritatively. 
Therefore, the Registry to place the
matter before Hon’ble The Chief Justice of
India to constitute a larger bench to consider
the question of law as mentioned above by an
appropriate Bench.”
2. Only  yesterday,  i.e.  25.11.2026,  this  Bench
delivered a judgment in Civil Appeal No. 14679 of 2026,
titled “Sukumarbai and Ors. Vs. United India Insurance
Company Ltd. And Anr.” relating to the coverage under
the “Act Only” policy.
3. The issue arising in the present matter is an
offshoot/ancillary to the judgment delivered yesterday
in the aforementioned case.
4. We have apprised the issue to the learned counsel(s)
appearing for the parties. They have prayed for a week’s
time to examine the issue and make their respective
submissions.
5. Let this matter be listed again as part-heard before
this Bench on 02.12.2026.
6

## Page 328

6. Learned counsel(s) for the parties shall come up
ready with the updated brief submissions on the next
date of hearing.

O R D E R
Heard learned counsel for the parties.
2. The issue which now remains to be gone into is with
regard to the handing over of the possession to the members of
the Appellant-Association specifically members No.24, 39 and 41
in the present case and the modalities with regard to the
payment which is required to be made by the respondent-Builder
in view of delay in handing over of possession.
3. After making arguments at length, both sides have agreed
that the matter can be disposed of in terms of the order passed
by a three-Judge Bench of this Court in the case of Santhosh
Narasimha Murthy & Ors. vs. M/s Mantri Castles Private Limited
&  Anr. dated  July  25,  2023  [Civil  Appeal  No.8418/2022]
specially the operative portion at paragraph No.17 thereof
which is extracted as under:

## Page 331

3
“17. We accordingly allow the appeal filed by the home
buyers in the following terms : 
(i) The home buyers shall be paid compensation on
account of delayed possession at the rate of Rs 3
per square foot per month in terms of clause 14.5
of the buyer agreements.
(ii) For computing the amount due under clause 14.5
in  terms  of  (i)  above,  the  assured  dates  of
possession, as reflected in Annexure P-14, shall be
the dates with effect from which the payment would
be  computed.  The  compensation  shall  be  payable
until 31 January 2023.
(iii) The home buyers shall be entitled to interest
at the rate of 6% per annum with effect from the
respective dates fixed for handing over possession,
as reflected in Annexure P-14; and
(iv) The amounts which are due and payable in the
above terms shall be paid over on or before 30
September 2023.”
4.  Having regard to the aforesaid, the present appeal
stands disposed of in terms of the aforesaid order dated July
25, 2023 passed by three-Judge Bench of this Court in Civil
Appeal No.8418/2022 and the direction issued at paragraph No.17
thereof shall operate in the present case also. However, the
Court clarifies that the members No.24, 39 and 41 shall be
handed over possession upon them paying the entire dues as per
the agreement entered between the parties, within six weeks
from today. Thereafter, the builder shall compute the accounts
and come up with a figure with regard to whatever amount
remains to be paid by the concerned members to the builder or
by  the  builder  to  the  concerned  members  of  the  present
Association in terms of the order dated July 25, 2023. The said
be  furnished  within  four  weeks  thereafter.  The  final
transaction be concluded within the next four weeks.

## Page 332

4
5. We clarify that with regard to member No.24, the payment
which has been refunded by the builder to him amounting to
Rs.75,91,723/-(Rupees Seventy-Five Lakhs, Ninety-one thousands,
Seven Hundred and Twenty-Three only), shall be paid by him to
the builder within two weeks and computation shall be made
treating the amount as not having been refunded to him.
6. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed
of.

1. Leave granted.
2. In the present case, this Court issued notice
on 05.06.2026, granting four weeks’ time to the
respondent-State  to  file  its  reply/counter-
affidavit.  Thereafter,  on  10.08.2026,  the
respondent-State again sought time to file its
reply/counter-affidavit.  However,  despite  the
opportunities granted, no reply/counter-affidavit
has been filed till date.
1

## Page 344

3. The present appeal has been preferred by the
appellant,  being  aggrieved  by  the  order  dated
05.02.2026 passed by the High Court of Calcutta in
CRAN  No.  4  of  2025,  whereby  the  appellant’s
application  seeking  suspension  of  sentence  was
rejected.
4. The appellant stands convicted by the Trial
Court for the offence punishable under Section 302
read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code,
1860,  and  has  been  sentenced  to  undergo
imprisonment  for  life.  The  criminal  appeal
preferred by the appellant challenging the judgment
of conviction and order of sentence is pending
consideration before the High Court. The appellant
has, thus far, undergone approximately 11 years of
rigorous imprisonment.
5. Learned counsel appearing for the appellant
submits that the incident occurred all of a sudden
in the course of an altercation and that, having
regard to the statements of the witnesses recorded
during the trial, the appellant has substantial
2

## Page 345

grounds to succeed in the criminal appeal. It is
further submitted that criminal appeal before the
High  Court  of  Calcutta  is  likely  to  take
considerable time for final disposal and that,
notwithstanding the pendency of the substantive
appeal,  the  appellant’s  application  seeking
suspension of sentence was rejected by the High
Court vide order dated 05.02.2026. Learned counsel
further submits that the appellant was earlier
released on interim bail and did not misuse the
liberty so granted to him.
6. Per contra, learned counsel appearing for the
respondent-State has vehemently opposed the prayer
for suspension of sentence and release of the
appellant on bail.
7. Having heard learned counsel for the parties
and upon perusal of the record, considering the
prolonged period of incarceration already undergone
by the appellant and the fact that the appeal
before the High Court is not likely to be heard in
the near future, this Court is of the opinion that
3

## Page 346

the prayer for suspension of sentence deserves to
be allowed.
8. Accordingly, the substantive sentence imposed
upon the appellant is suspended during the pendency
of the criminal appeal before the High Court. The
appellant shall be released on bail, subject to
such terms and conditions as may be imposed by the
Trial Court.
9. The High Court is requested to take up and
decide the pending criminal appeal at an early
date. The appellant shall not seek any adjournment
on the date(s) fixed for final hearing of the
appeal. It is made clear that, in the event the
appellant  seeks  an  adjournment  without  any
justifiable or cogent reason, the High Court shall
be at liberty to cancel the bail granted to the
appellant without seeking any further leave from
this Court.
10. The appeal is allowed in the above terms.

Leave granted.
2. The  plaintiffs  are  the  respondent  Nos.1  and  2  and  the
defendant is the  appellant  herein.  The  plaintiffs  filed  a  suit  for
specific  performance  on  the  strength  of  an  agreement  for  sale
dated  07.04.2006  preceded  by  an  earnest  money  deposit
evidenced by a receipt dated 07.02.2006 (visar pavati).
3. Three Courts concurrently found in favour of the plaintiffs and
Page 1/5

## Page 358

the  defendant  is  the  owner  of  the  properties.  At  the  time  of
admission, we issued notice only to see whether the compensation
amount  could  be  enhanced,  considering  the  fact  that  the
agreement was of the year 2006.
4. Even on the last occasion, we had put a query to the learned
Counsel  for  the  appellant  and  the  learned  Counsel  for  the
respondents. Learned Counsel for the defendant/respondent No.1
and  2  offered  to  raise  the  consideration  but  on  behalf  of  the
appellant, a higher offer was made.
5. Today when the matter was taken up the learned Counsel
appearing for  the respondent Nos.1 and 2,  agreed to  raise the
consideration to Rs.32 lakhs.  It is also pointed out by the learned
Counsel  that  at  the  time  of  admission,  this  Court  had  clearly
indicated  that  there  is  no  reason  to  cause  interference  to  the
impugned judgment on merits. Notice was issued only to explore
the possibility of enhancing the consideration amount, which the
respondent Nos.1 and 2 are agreeable to.
6. Learned  Senior  Counsel  appearing  for  the  appellant would,
Page 2/5

## Page 359

however,  submit  that  the  appellant  has  already  filed  an
undertaking before this Court to pay an amount of Rs.45 lakhs to
the respondent Nos.1 and 2, the plaintiffs, within a period of 30
days from the date of passing of order by this Court, subject to the
respondent Nos.1 and 2 giving up all their claims, interest and
rights on the property in question i.e. land bearing Survey No.15,
Hissa No.8/2 total admeasuring 00 H 40R, situated at village Warje,
Tal. Haveli, District Pune.
7. It is trite that specific performance is a discretionary remedy
and  in  the  present  case,  obviously,  the  price  of  the  land  has
increased  astronomically  as  is  evidenced  from  the  offer  and
counter-offer made by the parties. As submitted by the learned
Counsel for the respondent Nos.1 and 2, they have been litigating
for the past 20 years and should be permitted to enjoy the fruits of
their  labour.  However,  in  adjusting  equities,  the concern  of the
appellant,  who  was  the  defendants  and  original  owner  of  the
properties has also to be addressed. It is pointed out by learned
Counsel for the respondent Nos.1 and 2 that though the appellants
Page 3/5

## Page 360

are in possession of the property, thus are not residing there and
has leased out the same. This, however, does not persuade us to
digress  from  the  endeavour  to  settle  the  matter  amicably  on
principles of equity, exercising our discretion. Considering the offer
and  counter-offer  made,  we  are  of  the  opinion  that  the
plaintiffs/respondent Nos.1 and 2; who would have, in a decree of
refund obtained only the advance amount with reasonable interest,
is now being compensated with 45 Lakhs.
8. We are hence persuaded to accept the offer of the appellant
herein, who shall pay the amount as undertaken before this Court,
on or before 08.01.2027 to the account of the respondent Nos.1
and 2, who shall provide the details to the appellant. If the details
of the account of the respondent Nos.1 and 2 is not provided, then
the appellant would be enabled to make the deposit of the said
amount  before  this  Court  within  the  time  provided.  On  such
amounts being deposited, the judgment and decree of the Trial
Court and the Appellate Court shall stand set aside. If the amount is
not so deposited, the plaintiffs definitely would be entitled to move
Page 4/5

## Page 361

for execution, on the enhanced consideration of Rs.32 lakhs, minus
the advanced amount already paid.
9. The appeal stands disposed of with the above directions and
observations and the matter shall be posted on 12.01.2027 only to
ascertain the settlement having been carried out.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.              OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO. 17154/2026)
SHANKAR MAHTO & ORS.      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
THE STATE OF JHARKHAND & ANR.      RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant,
learned counsel for Respondent No.1-State of Jharkhand and
learned counsel for Respondent No.2-informant.
3. There are three appellants in this appeal. They are
Shankar Mahto, Rathu Mahto and Rajendra Gope @ Rajendra
Mahto.
4. Learned counsel for the appellants, at the very
outset, submits that Appellant No.1, Shankar Mahto, has
passed away during pendency of the Special Leave Petition.
5. The appellants are aggrieved by the order dated
06.05.2026 passed by the High Court of Jharkhand at Ranchi
(briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter), rejecting the
prayer for anticipatory bail of the appellants.
6. Be it stated that the three appellants along with
1

## Page 365

four others have been named as accused in FIR No.36/2021
registered at Police Station- Mandar, District- Ranchi,
Jharkhand under Sections 147, 148, 149, 341, 323, 427, 504
and 506 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, ‘IPC’)
and  Section  3(1)(r)(w)  of  the  Scheduled  Castes  and
Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 (for
short, ‘SC/ST Act’).
7. Allegation against the accused is that on 22.02.2021
at around 11:15 AM, accused along with 25-30 unknown
persons came near the house of the informant and destroyed
fruits and eggs kept in her property for the purpose of
sale. They also demolished the boundary wall of her house
while uttering words offensive to her caste.
8. The  High  Court,  vide  the  impugned  order  dated
06.05.2026, granted the benefit of pre-arrest bail to 04
of the accused while declining the same in respect of the
present appellants.
9. This Court, by order dated 07.09.2026, had issued
notice and granted interim protection to the appellants
subject  to  the  appellants  co-operating  with  the
investigation. It was further directed that the appellants
should submit an undertaking before the Investigating
Officer that they would not cause any harassment to the
informant during pendency of investigation and subsequent
trial, if the matter reaches the stage of trial. This
Court  clarified  that  any  instance  of  the  appellants
causing  harassment  to  the  informant  would  lead  to
2

## Page 366

cancellation of the bail granted to them.
10. Pursuant to notice issued by this Court, Respondent
No.1-State of Jharkhand and Respondent No.2-informant have
filed counter affidavits which we have perused.
11. Learned counsel for the appellants submits that the
High  Court  had  erred  in  rejecting  the  prayer  for
anticipatory bail of the appellants, inasmuch as the
allegation against all the accused persons is the same.
While four of the accused persons were granted the benefit
of pre-arrest bail, the same has been denied to the
appellants without any justification. She further submits
that pursuant to the interim protection granted by this
Court, appellants have joined investigation.
12. Learned  counsel  for  Respondent  No.1-State  of
Jharkhand while referring to the averments made in the
counter affidavit submits that appellants have joined
investigation.
13. On the other hand, learned counsel for Respondent
No.2-informant  vehemently  opposed  the  submission  of
learned counsel for the appellants. He submits that the
High Court was fully justified in rejecting the prayer for
anticipatory bail of the appellants. Unlike the four co-
accused, appellants were responsible for demolishing the
boundary wall of the informant, which fact was noted by
the High Court. Referring to the object of the SC/ST Act,
he submits that the same has been enacted to offer
protection to the marginalized and vulnerable sections of
3

## Page 367

the society. Under the SC/ST Act, there is no provision
for granting anticipatory bail. He, therefore, submits
that the appeal may be dismissed.
14. Submissions made by learned counsel for the parties
have received the due consideration of the Court.
15. While we concur with the sentiments expressed by
learned counsel for Respondent No.2-informant but at the
same  time,  the  Court  has  also  to  see  whether  the
allegation made in the FIR,  prima facie, attracts the
provisions of SC/ST Act. Of course, this is a matter for
trial  but  for  the  purpose  of  considering  bail  or
anticipatory bail, certainly the Court is entitled to look
into the substance of the accusations and take a prima
facie view.
16. On  a  query  by  the  Court,  learned  counsel  for
Respondent No.2-informant submits that Respondent No.2 has
not assailed the benefit of pre-arrest bail granted to the
other accused persons.
17. Be that as it may, having regard to the fact that the
appellants have co-operated with the investigation, we are
of the view that the interim protection granted by this
Court vide order dated 07.09.2026 should be made absolute.
18. That being the position, we set aside the impugned
order dated 06.05.2026 passed by the High Court qua the
appellants and make our order dated 07.09.2026 absolute,
subject to the condition that appellants shall continue to
co-operate with the investigation and shall not cause any
4

## Page 368

harassment to the informant.
19. Consequently, the Criminal Appeal is allowed.
20. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

agricultural purposes under the Jawan Lease Scheme, 
pursuant to the Government of Odisha’s policy dated 10th 
December, 1962. (Letter No. L.R.173/62/5799-R). 

## Page 383

C.A. @ SLP (C.) No. 12651 of 2021  Page 2 
 
 
3.2.The Tahsildar, Khallikote, informed him that no 
Government land was available in the Tehsil and advised 
him to select land in another Tehsil. Thereafter, he shifted 
to Berhampur with his family.  
3.3.In 1980, appellant’s father applied to the Tahsildar, 
Berhampur, for settlement of 5 acres of land at Palur Hills 
under Khata No. 42, which was reserved for settlement in 
favour of Jawans. He also fenced and took possession of 
the land. Subsequently he passed away on 02nd June, 
1992. 
3.4.Upon the creation of Konisi Tehsil in 1995, Palur Hills 
came within its jurisdiction. The relevant records were 
accordingly transferred to the Tahsildar, Konisi, for 
further action. 
3.5.In 1998, the Tahsildar, Konisi, initiated Jawan Lease 
Case No. 02/98 in the name of the appellant’s mother and 
commenced an enquiry. However, by order dated 21st 
October, 1998, the proceedings were dropped on the 
ground that Palur Hills was beyond the prescribed 5 km 
radius from Berhampur.  
3.6.The appellant’s mother passed away on 08th February, 
2002. Following her death, the appellant learnt of the 
order dated 21st October, 1998, whereby the Jawan Lease 
proceedings had been dropped. He challenged the said 

## Page 384

C.A. @ SLP (C.) No. 12651 of 2021  Page 3 
 
order before the Additional Sub-Collector, Berhampur, 
and the appeal was registered as Jawan Appeal No. 1. 
3.7.By order dated 13th February, 2009, the Additional Sub-
Collector set aside the order dated 21st October, 1998, 
holding that the proceedings had been dropped without 
affording the appellant’s mother an opportunity of 
hearing. The matter was remanded to the Tahsildar for 
fresh enquiry and consideration of the claim for settlement 
of the land. 
3.8.As the Tahsildar did not act pursuant to the remand 
order, the appellant approached the High Court by filing 
W.P. No. 8473/2014. By order dated 13th November, 
2014, the High Court directed the Tahsildar to dispose of 
Jawan Lease Case No. 02/98 within four months from the 
date of production of a certified copy of the order. 
3.9.However, by order dated 16th December, 2014, the 
Tahsildar stated that the case had already been disposed 
of as non-maintainable on 31st July, 2014. 
3.10.Aggrieved thereby, the appellant filed W.P.(C) No. 
19411/2015 before the High Court, challenging the order 
dated 16th December, 2014. The High Court disposed of 
the writ petition by the impugned judgment dated 18th 
March, 2021. 
 
4. Vide the impugned order, the High Court disposed off the writ 
petition noting that the policy of the State with regard to 

## Page 385

C.A. @ SLP (C.) No. 12651 of 2021  Page 4 
 
allotment of land under Jawan Lease System has been 
changed and is now to give cash incentive, therefore, the 
relief prayed for cannot be granted.  
 
5. We have heard learned counsels for the parties and perused 
the material available on record. 
 
6. Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that the 
appellant’s claim was required to be considered in terms of 
the Government of Odisha’s policy dated 10th December, 
1962, which was in force at the time of the application. It was 
contended that the Home Department, by its communication 
dated 05th August, 1980, had specifically directed the 
Collector, Ganjam, to allot land to the appellant’s father. 
However, no steps were taken to give effect to the said 
direction. It was urged that the appellant’s claim could not 
be defeated by the authorities ’prolonged inaction. Learned 
counsel further submitted that the High Court, by a brief 
order, declined relief solely on the ground of a subsequent 
change in policy, without examining the earlier Government 
direction or the orders passed by the Additional Sub-
Collector in favour of the appellant. 
 
7. Per contra, learned counsel for the respondents opposed the 
appellant’s claim for allotment of the land. It was submitted 
that the appellant had encroached upon the Government 
land by fencing it, without awaiting a decision on his 

## Page 386

C.A. @ SLP (C.) No. 12651 of 2021  Page 5 
 
application for settlement. The land at Palur Hills is classified 
as Parvat Kissa and is hilly and rocky, rendering it 
unsuitable for agricultural purposes. It was further 
contended that the land is earmarked for Government and 
developmental purposes and has been allotted for projects 
including Khallikote Junior College and a Driving Training 
School. It was further submitted that the Jawan Lease 
Scheme had subsequently been revised by Government 
Resolution dated 19th February, 2014, under which cash 
incentives were provided in place of land allotment.  
 
8. Upon hearing learned counsel for the parties and examining 
the material on record, we are of the view that the matter 
calls for fresh consideration by the High Court. The 
impugned judgment does not reflect due consideration of the 
various issues arising for determination or the rival claims 
advanced by the parties. We are, therefore, of the considered 
opinion that the matter ought to be reconsidered by the High 
Court after taking into account the respective submissions 
and the material on record.  
 
9. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. The impugned judgment 
is set aside and the matter is remitted to the High Court for 
fresh consideration and decision in accordance with law. We 
clarify that we have not expressed any opinion on the merits 
of the matter, and all contentions are left open. 

## Page 387

C.A. @ SLP (C.) No. 12651 of 2021  Page 6 
 
10. Having regard to the fact that the matter is an old one and 
concerns allotment of land under the Jawan Lease Scheme 
pursuant to the Government policy dated 10th December, 
1962, we request the High Court to consider expeditious 
disposal of the writ petition. Both parties shall extend their 
full cooperation in ensuring its expeditious disposal. 
 
11. Pending application (s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Civil Appeal No.      /2026
(Arising out of SLP (C) No.39493/2026)
GURMEET KAUR                                          Appellant
                                VERSUS
HONEY CHAHAL & ORS.                                   Respondents
O R D E R
1. Leave granted. 
2. We have heard Mr. Mukul Rohatgi learned senior counsel, for
the appellant and Ms. Shumaila Altaf, learned counsel appearing on
behalf of first respondent.
3. During the course of the arguments, it was submitted by
learned  senior  Counsel  as  well  as  learned  counsel  for  the
respective parties that the suit filed by the appellant herein
i.e., Civil Suit No. 2044/2023 which was decreed in favour of the
appellant, was appealed against by the first respondent and the
Appellate Court has remanded the matter to the trial Court for the
purpose of granting a fresh opportunity to the respondent herein
(defendant in the suit) to let in further evidence. The said suit
is pending adjudication before the trial Court on remand.
4. It was also pointed out that F.A.O. 5980/2024 (O&M), pending
before  the  Punjab  and  Haryana  High  Court,  arises  out  of  a
1

## Page 395

guardianship proceeding which was filed by respondent No.1 herein,
who is the biological mother of the minor child, namely, Agam
Pratap Singh, who is presently seven years of age. Since respondent
No.1 herein was unsuccessful in the said guardianship proceeding,
she was constrained to file the appeal, which is pending before the
High Court. Against the interim order dated 19.12.2024 passed by
the High Court, this appeal has been filed, after hearing, the same
is stayed.
5. Learned counsel for the first respondent also brought to our
notice order dated 03.11.2026 passed by the High Court in F.A.O.
No.5980/2024 (O&M) in which an earlier order dated 28.08.2023
passed in CRWP-8930/2022 was replicated that the respondent No.1
has visitation rights on every Saturday and Sunday and respondent
No.1 has right to visit the child in terms of the direction issued
therein. For ease of reference, we extract the said direction which
reads thus:-
“25. Court is also informed that petitioner no.2,
the  biological  father  of  the  minor  child,  is
presently out of India on one year fellowship in USA
for a super specialized course in Radiology. Be that
as it may, in the larger interest of welfare of the
child and in fairness to the contesting parties
herein, taking guidance from the Apex Court judgment
rendered in Tejaswani Gauds ibid, it is directed
that, as an interim measure, the adoptive mother
shall  allow  the  biological  parents  to  have  the
visitation rights qua the minor child, Master Agam
Pratap Singh on every weekend. For this, respondent
No.3 will ensure that the minor is dropped on every
Saturday by 11:00 a.m. at the residence of petitioner
No.1-Dr. Honey Chahal. Likewise Dr. Honey Chahal
shall ensure that on every next Sunday the minor is
2

## Page 396

dropped back at the residence of respondent No.3 by
06:00 p.m. The child is stated to be enrolled in a
school/play school. It is not clear if school is five
or six days in week. Assuming, it is six days, given
that child is at nursery/kindergarten level, no harm
would be caused if for few months he does not attend
the school on Saturdays on the weekends. Parties are
directed to comply with the direction of this court
in mutual spirit of give and take keeping their
differences aside and in the larger interest of
welfare of the child. They all must make earnest
collective endeavour to ensure that the minor is not
subjected  to  any  distress  or  anguish  on  their
account, which may lead to him being inconsolable,
given his tender age. State and concerned SSP are
since arrayed as respondents herein, they are also
directed  to  ensure  the  compliance.  Should  the
unlikely situation arise, parties are at liberty to
seek police assistance for enforcement of the interim
arrangement. But it shall be ensured that only lady
officials, that too in plain clothes and not in the
police uniform are deputed for the purpose.”
6. Learned counsel for respondent No.1 further submitted that the
said order was also sustained by this Court  vide  order dated
28.01.2026. That on remand the trial Court has to adjudicate on the
validity of the so-called adoption sought for by the appellant
herein and in the circumstances the aforesaid interim arrangement
may be continued. 
7. However,  learned  senior  counsel  contended  that  the  said
interim arrangement is not in the best interest of the child
inasmuch as the respondent No.1 presently resides at Hoshiarpur and
the appellant along with the child reside at Ludhiana.
8. In these circumstances, we modify the order dated 19.12.2024
by way of an interim arrangement, we permit the respondent No.1 to
3

## Page 397

exercise her visitation rights vis-a-vis, of minor child on the 1st
and 3rd weekends of every month and the 2nd, 4th and 5th weekends, if
any, of every month the child shall remain in the custody of the
appellant herein.
9. We clarify that this interim arrangement is in the interest of
the minor child and on 1st and 3rd weekend of every month the said
respondent can take the child to Hoshiarpur and the directions
issued in CRWP No.8930-2022 which have been replicated in the order
dated 19.12.2024 stand modified, accordingly.
10. As far as the ensuing winter vacation is concerned 1st half of
the winter vacation shall be spent with the respondent No.1 and the
2nd half will be with the appellant.
11. In view of the aforesaid, the proceedings in FAO No.5980/2024
out of which this Special Leave Petition arises, shall remain
stayed. We say so, for the reason, that the suit between the
parties is pending adjudication on remand.
12. Learned Senior Counsel, Mr. Mukul Rohatgi further submitted
that the review petition filed by the appellant against the order
of remand before the District Court shall be withdrawn. His
submission is placed on record.
13. The Civil Suit No. 2044/2023 pending between the parties,
shall be disposed of on or before 31st March, 2027.
4

## Page 398

14. Accordingly, this civil appeal stands disposed of.
Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

            Being aggrieved by  order dated  26.10.2026 passed by 
the Bombay High Court in Writ Petition (L) No. 35535/2026,  
the petitioner has preferred this Special Leave Petition  
seeking  permission  for  medical  termination  of  her  
pregnancy under Section 3(2)(b) of the Medical Termination  
of Pregnancy Act, 1971 (hereinafter referred to as the `MTP 
Act’).
The impugned order is dated 26.10.2026 by which the  
petitioner’s prayer for seeking termination of pregnancy  
(presently  25  weeks)  made  under  Article  226  of  the  
Constitution of India was rejected. This Special leave  
Petition was filed on 27.10.2026.
We heard learned counsel for the petitioner and learned 
counsel for respondent No.2-husband/Caveator and learned  
counsel for respondent No.1/State, who appeared on advance 
notice (on 29.10.2026).
Thereafter, the matter was listed on 02.11.2026 and we 
heard learned counsel for the respective parties extensively 
in the presence of the petitioner and respondent No.2, who 
appeared through Video Conferencing facility and the matter 
was directed to be listed today (04.11.2026) at 02.00 P.M. 
We have heard learned counsel for the respective parties 
in the presence of the petitioner, who has appeared through 
2

## Page 408

Video Conferencing facility and respondent No.2, who has  
appeared in person. 
Having  taken note of the submissions advanced at the Bar
on behalf of the respective parties, we find that having  
regard to the facts and circumstances of this case, the  
prayer sought for by the petitioner herein cannot be granted.
The Special Leave Petition is hence dismissed.
All pleadings filed during the course of hearing before 
this Court shall not be construed to the prejudice of the 
respective parties in any other proceeding.
