IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
ARBITRATION PETITION NO. 46 OF 2026
AUREUS ANALYTICS LIMITED & 
ORS.
PETITIONER(S)
VERSUS
GRADATIM I.T. VENTURES 
PRIVATE LIMITED & ORS.
RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. The present petition has been filed under Section 11(6) read
with Section 11(12)(a) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act,
1996 (“1996 Act”), seeking the appointment of a Sole Arbitrator to
adjudicate the disputes that have arisen between the parties.
2. Briefly stated, Petitioner No. 1 is a company incorporated
under the laws of Singapore, and Petitioner Nos. 2 to 5 are
individuals.  The  Petitioners  held  the  entire  shareholding  of
Respondent No. 3, a company incorporated in India and engaged in
providing Software as a Service (SaaS) for persistency, claims and
fraud analytics in the insurance sector. Respondent No. 1 is a
company incorporated in India, and Respondent No. 2 is stated to be
its Founder and CEO.
3. By a Share Purchase Agreement dated 12.04.2024 (“SPA”) and a
Side Agreement of the same date (“Side Agreement”) (collectively,
“Agreements”), the Petitioners sold their entire shareholding in
Respondent No. 3 to Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 for a purchase
1

## Page 419

consideration of Rs. 1,04,51,740/-. Under the Side Agreement, a
further  consideration  of  Rs.  60,00,000/-  was  payable  to  the
Petitioners, which Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 were entitled to retain
as the Hold Back Amount for a period of one year from the Closing
Date, to meet any claims or losses arising from the Hold Back
Events specified therein, and to release the balance, if any,
thereafter. According to the Petitioners, the Closing Date was
16.04.2024.
4. Clause 14.2 of the SPA provides that disputes which are not
resolved amicably shall be referred to binding arbitration by a
Sole Arbitrator, to be mutually appointed by the parties within 30
days of the Arbitration Notice and, failing such agreement, to be
appointed in accordance with the 1996 Act. The seat of arbitration
is Mumbai, Maharashtra, and the language of the arbitration is
English. The Side Agreement incorporates the terms and conditions
of the SPA by reference.
5. It is the Petitioners’ case that the Hold Back Period expired
on 16.04.2025 without any claim having been raised in respect of
the  Hold  Back  Events,  and  that  the  Hold  Back  Amount  has
nevertheless  not  been  released  despite  their  e-mail  dated
01.05.2025 and the discussions held between July and October 2025.
Respondent No. 2, by e-mail dated 02.05.2025, asserted that the
targets relating to revenue and customer numbers had not been met.
6. The  Petitioners,  by  notice  dated  09.12.2025,  invoked
2

## Page 420

arbitration under Clause 14.2 of the SPA and proposed the name of
an Advocate as the Sole Arbitrator. By reply dated 07.01.2026,
Respondent No. 1 disputed the claim, stated that the amount payable
by it was Rs. 33,15,366/- as against the claim of Rs. 60,00,000/-,
objected to the Petitioners’ nominee and proposed another Advocate
as the Sole Arbitrator. The parties having failed to agree on the
appointment, the Petitioners have filed the present petition.
7. We have heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the
material placed on record. Since Petitioner No. 1 is a body
corporate  incorporated  in  a  country  other  than  India,  the
arbitration is an international commercial arbitration within the
meaning of Section 2(1)(f)(ii) of the 1996 Act. This Court,
therefore, has jurisdiction under Section 11(6) read with Section
11(12)(a) of the 1996 Act.
8. The existence of the arbitration agreement is not in dispute,
and the parties differ only on the person to be appointed as the
Sole Arbitrator. The parties have placed their suggestions as to
who may be appointed as a Sole Arbitrator. In the alternative, it
was proposed that an Arbitrator from the panel of the Mumbai Centre
for International Arbitration may be appointed.
9. In view of the above, the petition is allowed. In light of the
submission of the parties, we request the Mumbai Centre for
International  Arbitration  to  appoint  a  Sole  Arbitrator  to
adjudicate the disputes between the parties arising out of the
3

## Page 421

Agreements. The seat and venue of arbitration shall be Mumbai.
10. The learned Sole Arbitrator shall fix the fee and other
modalities of the arbitration in consultation with the parties. The
appointment  shall  be  subject  to  the  learned  Sole  Arbitrator
furnishing the disclosure required under Section 12(1) read with
the Sixth Schedule to the 1996 Act, and there being no legal
impediment to the appointment.
11. All rights and contentions of the parties on merits, including
their respective claims, counterclaims and defences, are left open.
The observations made hereinabove are only for the purpose of
deciding this petition and shall not influence the learned Sole
Arbitrator.
12. The arbitration petition is allowed in the above terms.
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.        OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP (Criminal) No. 17341 of 2026)
ARSHAD  APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
STATE OF UP RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, by
the impugned judgment and order dated 27.04.2026, has
rejected the appellant’s prayer for bail.
3. Appellant, is figuring as an accused in FIR
No.269 of 2025, registered at Police Station Budhana,
District Muzaffarnagar, under Sections 64(1), 333 and
115(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
4. The petitioner has been in custody for about
one and a half years.
5. Learned counsel appearing for the appellant
1

## Page 431

submits  that  the  appellant  has  been  falsely
implicated in the present case and has not committed
the alleged offence. It is further submitted that as
many as 12 family members were residing in the house
of the prosecutrix, making it improbable that the
entire house and the neighbourhood were deserted at
the relevant time. Learned counsel further submits
that, owing to a previous scuffle between the father
of the prosecutrix and the father of the appellant, a
false and concocted FIR came to be registered against
the appellant. It is also contended that there is no
medical evidence corroborating the prosecution case.
Learned counsel further points out that, out of the
22 prosecution witnesses cited, only one witness has
been examined so far.
6. Per contra, learned counsel appearing for the
respondent-State has vehemently opposed the prayer
for grant of bail, contending that, having regard to
the gravity of the allegations, no case for grant of
bail is made out.
7. Having heard learned counsel for the parties
2

## Page 432

and upon perusal of the material on record, and
considering the period of custody already undergone
by the appellant as well as the fact that the trial
is likely to take considerable time to conclude, we
are of the opinion that the appellant deserves to be
enlarged on bail.
8. Accordingly,  we  set  aside  the  impugned
judgment and order of the High Court.
9. Appellant shall be released on bail, subject
to furnishing of bail bonds to the satisfaction of
the trial court and subject to such other terms and
conditions as may be imposed by it.
10. Needless to observe, the appellant shall not,
directly or indirectly, by making inducement, threat
or promise, dissuade any person acquainted with the
facts of the case from disclosing such facts to the
court.
11. In the event there is any breach of the terms
and conditions for grant of bail, the trial court
shall be at liberty to cancel the bail of the
appellant.
3

## Page 433

12. It is also ordered that the appellant shall
diligently attend proceedings of the trial, unless
exempted. If he is found to abstain from attending
the proceedings without justifiable cause, that could
also be seen as breach of the conditions for grant of
bail and the trial court will be free to pass
appropriate orders.
13. We clarify that the observations made in this
order and grant of bail will not be treated as
findings on the merits of the case.
14. The appeal is, accordingly, allowed on the
aforesaid terms.
15. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

“2. ...For the reasons to follow, we disagree

21.  Thus,  the  following  principles  can  be
culled  out  on  the  basis  of  the  decisions
surveyed:
(i) The Judiciary alone has the responsibility
of authoritatively interpreting legislation and
determining its legal meaning while deciding
individual cases before it. This function is
the exclusive province of constitutional courts
and any explanation or meaning found by any
2 of 5

## Page 450

Civil Appeal  No(s).  410/2023 etc.
other  agency  is  always  subject  to  the
interpretation of constitutional courts.
(ii) Constitutional courts primarily adopt the
plain and natural meaning of the language used
in the legislation. If the intention of the
legislature is not conveyed expressly, clearly,
and completely, the court will declare the
intention  by  interpreting  the  text  in  its
context and in the light of the purpose and
object of the legislation. Further, the court
may adopt an external aid to decipher the
meaning of the legislation, with one of them
being subordinate legislation made under the
primary statute.1
(iii) While using subordinate legislation to
interpret the provisions of a primary statute,
constitutional courts must bear in mind that,
by its very nature, subordinate legislation is
founded on the Executive Branch’s understanding
of  the  primary  legislation.  To  adopt  that
position uncritically would be to substitute
the rule-making authority for the court as the
interpreter. Further, this would disregard the
possibility  of  the  subordinate  legislation
being misconceived or ultra vires the statute.
(iv) Subordinate legislation, by itself, does
not determine or control the meaning of the
primary statute. It can only be an aid to
supplement or corroborate a meaning that a
constitutional court would have found on the
basis of other interpretative criteria.  It
cannot  oust  a  meaning  that  the  statutory
provision could bear, unless that is supported
by the statutory scheme itself, read with the
purpose and object of the legislation.
(v) Contemporaneously made rules could aid in
understanding the width of certain expressions
used  in  the  statute  to  indicate  its
inclusiveness.  Subordinate  legislation,  by
itself, however, cannot restrict the meaning of
the words used in the primary legislation.
22.  Keeping  in  mind  the  above-referred
principles, Rules 4A to 4C, as inserted by the

challenge  in  these  proceedings  and,  more

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA

SONICA SHUKLA & ORS. APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
THE NATIONAL INSURANCE CO. LTD
& ANR.
RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. This appeal, at the instance of the claimants, arises from the
judgment dated 24.08.2023 (“impugned judgment”) of the High Court
of Judicature at Allahabad (“High Court”) in First Appeal From
Order No. 269 of 2009. In that judgment, the High Court partly
allowed  the  Appellants’  appeal  and  enhanced  the  compensation
awarded  by  the  Motor  Accident  Claims  Tribunal,  Kanpur  Dehat
(“Tribunal”), vide award dated 29.09.2008 (“Award”), in Motor
Accident Claim Petition No. 126 of 2007, from Rs. 4,17,500/- to Rs.
7,75,600/-.  The  Appellants  seek  further  enhancement  of  the
compensation.
3. Briefly stated, the Appellants are the widow (Appellant No.
1), the two children (Appellant Nos. 2 and 3) and the mother
(Appellant No. 4) of Sri Avinash Shukla, who died in a motor
vehicle accident on 27.01.2007. He was about 34 years old and ran a
photocopy and electronics shop. On that day, while he was returning
1

## Page 479

home  on  his  motorcycle,  an  Eicher  D.C.M.  truck  (“offending
vehicle”) collided with him near Riti Kirti Rice Mill, P.S.
Bhognipur, Kanpur Dehat. He was taken to L.L.R. Hospital, Kanpur,
where he succumbed to his injuries the same day. The offending
vehicle was insured with Respondent No. 1, The National Insurance
Co. Ltd. (“Insurer”).
4. The Appellants claimed compensation of Rs. 30,55,000/-. The
Tribunal assessed the income of the deceased at Rs. 3,000/- per
month, deducted one-third towards personal expenses and, applying a
multiplier  of  17,  computed  the  loss  of  dependency  at  Rs.
4,08,000/-. It further awarded Rs. 9,500/- under the conventional
heads, i.e., a total of Rs. 4,17,500/-, with interest at 6% per
annum from the date of the Award. Nothing was awarded towards
future prospects.
5. In the Appellants’ appeal, the High Court took the income of
the deceased at Rs. 3,500/- per month, added 40% towards future
prospects, deducted one-fourth towards personal expenses in view of
the four dependants, applied a multiplier of 16 and enhanced the
amount  under  the  conventional  heads  to  Rs.  70,000/-.  The
compensation was thus assessed at Rs. 7,75,600/-, with simple
interest at 6% per annum from the date of institution of the claim
petition till payment.
6. We have heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the
record. It is contended on behalf of the Appellants that the income
2

## Page 480

of the deceased was considerably higher than that assessed, and
that no separate compensation towards consortium was awarded to
each of the dependants.
7. The deceased was a young man of about 34 years running his own
business, and four persons, including his two children, who were
then minors, and his mother, were dependent on him. In these
circumstances, the assessment of his income at Rs. 3,500/- per
month  for  want  of  documentary  proof,  and  the  award  of  a
consolidated sum of Rs. 70,000/- under the conventional heads, do
not adequately reflect the loss suffered by the Appellants.
8. Keeping in view the age of the deceased, the number of his
dependants and the nature of his occupation, we deem it just and
proper to enhance the total compensation to Rs. 12,00,000/- (Rupees
Twelve Lakhs only), in place of Rs. 7,75,600/- awarded by the High
Court.
9. We are informed that the amount awarded by the High Court has
already been released. The Insurer shall, therefore, pay the
balance amount of Rs. 4,24,400/- (Rupees Four Lakhs Twenty-Four
Thousand Four Hundred only) to the Appellants within six weeks from
today. The amount shall be remitted directly into the bank accounts
of the Appellants, the particulars of which shall be furnished by
their learned counsel to learned counsel for the Insurer.
10. The appeal is allowed in the above terms. The Award, as
3

## Page 481

modified  by  the  impugned  judgment,  stands  further  modified
accordingly. There shall be no order as to costs.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA

(ARISING OUT OF SLP (CIVIL) NO. 20986 OF 2024)
VIRENDER SINGH APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
THE ORIENTAL INSURANCE CO. 
LTD. & ORS.
RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. This appeal, at the instance of the injured claimant, arises
from the judgment dated 20.09.2023 (“impugned judgment”) of the
High Court of Judicature at Allahabad (“High Court”) in First
Appeal From Order No. 1300 of 2001. In that judgment, the High
Court partly allowed the Appellant’s appeal and enhanced the
compensation  awarded  by  the  Additional  Motor  Accident  Claims
Tribunal, Etah (“Tribunal”), vide award dated 30.03.2001 (“Award”),
in Motor Accident Claim Petition No. 265 of 1994. The Appellant
seeks further enhancement of the compensation.
3. Briefly stated, on 26.10.1994, the Appellant, then about 25
years old and working as a mason, was riding pillion on a scooter
when a truck struck the scooter from behind. He fell onto the road,
and the truck ran over his arms. His right arm was amputated at the
shoulder, and his left arm suffered crush injuries below the elbow,
leaving it permanently disabled. He also sustained head injuries.
He had a wife and three minor children at the time.
4. The Appellant claimed compensation of Rs. 8,25,000/- with
interest. The Tribunal held the truck driver solely responsible for
1

## Page 484

the accident and fastened the liability on Respondent No. 1, The
Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. (“Insurer”), the insurer of the truck.
Assessing the Appellant’s income at Rs. 2,000/- per month and his
disability at 90%, and applying a multiplier of 17, it awarded Rs.
3,67,200/- towards loss of earning capacity. It further awarded Rs.
91,200/- towards medical expenses and Rs. 50,000/- towards pain and
suffering, i.e., a total of Rs. 5,08,400/-, with interest at 9% per
annum from 09.02.1999.
5. In the Appellant’s appeal, the High Court granted 40% towards
future prospects, applied a multiplier of 18 in place of 17, and
awarded Rs. 50,000/- towards medical expenses, Rs. 30,000/- towards
an attendant and Rs. 70,000/- towards pain and suffering. The
enhanced amount was to carry simple interest at 6% per annum from
the date of institution of the claim petition till payment.
6. We have heard learned counsel for the Appellant and the
Insurer  and  perused  the  record.  Respondent  No.  4,  National
Insurance Co. Ltd., the insurer of the scooter, is a  proforma
respondent against whom no relief is claimed.
7. While we see no reason to interfere with the assessment of
income, the compensation awarded under the non-pecuniary heads and
towards future care does not, in our view, constitute “just
compensation”. At about 25 years of age, the Appellant lost one arm
entirely, while the other was rendered virtually unproductive,
leaving him dependent on others for the rest of his life. Nothing
has been awarded towards loss of amenities and enjoyment of life,
and the amounts awarded towards pain and suffering and attendant
2

## Page 485

loss are inadequate. The Appellant has also waited over three
decades for this litigation to conclude.
8. We,  therefore,  deem  it  just  and  proper  to  enhance  the
compensation by a further sum of Rs. 5,00,000/- (Rupees Five Lakhs
only), over and above the compensation awarded by the High Court.
9. The Insurer shall pay the said amount to the Appellant within
eight weeks from today. The amount shall be remitted directly into
the bank account of the Appellant, the particulars of which shall
be furnished by his learned counsel to learned counsel for the
Insurer.
10. The appeal is allowed in the above terms. The Award, as
modified  by  the  impugned  judgment,  stands  further  modified
accordingly. There shall be no order as to costs.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

1. Leave granted.
2. This appeal, at the claimant’s instance, arises from the
judgment dated 08.11.2024 (“impugned judgment”) of the High Court
of Judicature for Rajasthan at Jodhpur (“High Court”) in S.B. Civil
Misc. Appeal No. 587 of 2016. In that judgment, the High Court
partly allowed the Appellant’s appeal and enhanced the compensation
awarded by the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (Labour Court), Sri
Ganganagar (“Tribunal”), vide award dated 08.01.2016 (“Award”) in
MAC Case No. 34 of 2010, from Rs. 2,50,000/- to Rs. 4,67,000/-. The
Appellant seeks further enhancement of the compensation.
3. Briefly stated, on 06.02.2009, at about 7:30 p.m., a jeep
bearing Registration No. RJ-13-C-4088, in which the Appellant’s
son, Puran Bhagat alias Purna Ram, was travelling with others to
Ramdeora, collided with a truck-trailer bearing Registration No.
PB-05L-9688 (“offending vehicle”), which had been parked in the
middle of the road about two kilometres beyond Village Nokhada
without any indicator or warning light. The Appellant’s son, then
12 years old and a student of the 6th standard, died on the spot,
1

## Page 489

along with three other occupants of the jeep. The offending vehicle
was insured with Respondent No. 3, The New India Assurance Co. Ltd.
(“Insurer”).
4. The Appellant, the sole claimant, claimed compensation of Rs.
39,50,000/-. The Tribunal awarded Rs. 2,50,000/-, over and above
the interim compensation of Rs. 50,000/- already paid, including
Rs. 75,000/- under the conventional heads, with interest at 9% per
annum from the date of filing of the claim petition. The liability
was fastened jointly and severally on the driver, the owner and the
Insurer of the offending vehicle.
5. In the Appellant’s appeal, the High Court took the notional
income of the deceased child at Rs. 30,000/- per annum, applied a
multiplier of 15 and awarded Rs. 67,000/- under the conventional
heads. After adjusting the interim compensation, the compensation
was assessed at Rs. 4,67,000/-, i.e., an enhancement of Rs.
2,17,000/-, with interest at 9% per annum from the date of filing
of the claim petition. The Insurer’s appeal against the Award was
dismissed.
6. We have heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the
record.
7. The Appellant is a widow who lost her 12-year-old son, a
school student, in the accident. Keeping in view the age of the
deceased, the loss suffered by the Appellant as his mother and the
lapse of more than seventeen years since the accident, we are of
the view that the compensation awarded by the High Court does not
constitute “just compensation”.

8. We,  therefore,  deem  it  just  and  proper  to  enhance  the
compensation by a further sum of Rs. 12,00,000/- (Rupees Twelve
Lakhs only), over and above the compensation awarded by the High
Court.

six weeks from today. The amount shall be remitted directly into
the bank account of the Appellant, the particulars of which shall
be furnished by her learned counsel to learned counsel for the
Insurer.

modified  by  the  impugned  judgment,  stands  further  modified

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.         OF 2026
(ARISING OUT OF SLP (CIVIL) NO. 30952 OF 2024)
KALASH JAISWAL APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
AMAR KUMAR CHOUDHARY & ANR. RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. This appeal, at the instance of the injured claimant, arises
from the judgment dated 29.08.2024 (“impugned judgment”) of the
High Court of Jharkhand at Ranchi (“High Court”) in Miscellaneous
Appeal No. 506 of 2019. In that judgment, the High Court partly
allowed  the  Appellant’s  appeal  and  enhanced  the  compensation
awarded by the Motor Vehicles Accident Claims Tribunal, Ranchi
(“Tribunal”), vide award dated 23.03.2017 (“Award”) in Compensation
Case No. 2 of 2008. The Appellant seeks further enhancement of the
compensation.
3. Briefly stated, on 15.01.2007, the Appellant, then about five
years old, was returning home from tuition classes in District
Khunti,  Jharkhand,  when  she  was  struck  by  a  truck  bearing
Registration No. BEN-6276 (“offending vehicle”), which ran over her
right foot. She was taken to the Sub-Divisional Hospital, Khunti,
referred to RIMS, Ranchi, and thereafter shifted to Nagarmal Modi
Sewa Sadan, Ranchi, for treatment. All five toes of her right foot
1

## Page 494

were amputated. As certified by the Civil Surgeon-cum-Chief Medical
Officer, Khunti, she has suffered a permanent 50% disability of her
right leg, which is non-progressive and not likely to improve.
Consequently, a criminal case was registered against the driver of
the offending vehicle under Sections 279, 337 and 338 of the Indian
Penal Code, 1860, and a chargesheet was filed.
4. The Appellant, then a minor, through her father and natural
guardian, claimed compensation of Rs. 5,00,000/- with interest.
Respondent No. 1, the owner of the offending vehicle, admitted
ownership and insurance, while Respondent No. 2, The New India
Assurance Co. Ltd. (“Insurer”), contested the claim. The Tribunal
held that the accident was caused by the rash and negligent driving
of the offending vehicle and fastened the liability on the Insurer.
Taking the Appellant’s notional income at Rs. 3,000/- per month,
i.e., Rs. 36,000/- per annum, and her functional disability at 50%,
it computed the loss of earnings at Rs. 2,70,000/- by applying a
multiplier of 15 to Rs. 18,000/- per annum. It further awarded Rs.
1,00,000/- towards pain and suffering, Rs. 2,00,000/- towards loss
of enjoyment of life and Rs. 39,928/- towards medical expenses,
i.e., a total of Rs. 6,09,928/-, with interest at 12% per annum
from the date of the Award. Interest for the period during which
the claim was pending was declined, as the delay was attributed to
the claimant.
5. In  the  Appellant’s  appeal,  the  High  Court  enhanced  the
compensation towards pain and suffering to Rs. 3,00,000/- and
2

## Page 495

towards loss of enjoyment of life to Rs. 5,00,000/-, retained the
loss  of  earning  at  Rs.  2,70,000/-,  and  recalculated  the
compensation at Rs. 10,70,000/-, with simple interest at 6% per
annum from the date of the accident till payment.
6. We have heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the
record. The occurrence of the accident and the liability of the
Insurer are not in dispute. The only question is the adequacy of
the compensation.
7. The Appellant was a child of tender age when she lost all five
toes of her right foot, and the resulting permanent disability will
remain with her for the rest of her life. Keeping in view her age
at the time of the accident, the nature of the injuries, the
permanent disability and the lapse of time, we deem it just and
proper to enhance the compensation to Rs. 12,00,000/- (Rupees
Twelve Lakhs only), in place of Rs. 10,70,000/- awarded by the High
Court. The enhanced amount shall carry simple interest at 6% per
annum from the date of the accident till payment, as directed by
the High Court.
8. The Insurer shall pay the enhanced compensation, along with
interest as aforesaid, to the Appellant within six weeks from
today, after adjusting any amount already paid or deposited. The
amount shall be remitted directly into the bank account of the
Appellant, who has since attained majority, the particulars of
which shall be furnished by her learned counsel to learned counsel
3

## Page 496

for the Insurer. In case of default, the amount of Rs. 12,00,000/-
shall carry additional simple interest at 6% per annum from the
expiry of the said period of six weeks till the date of payment.
9. The appeal is allowed in the above terms. The Award, as
modified  by  the  impugned  judgment,  stands  further  modified
accordingly. There shall be no order as to costs.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

4. This  appeal  arises  from  an  order
dated 10.09.2026 passed by the High Court of
Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur rejecting the
regular bail prayer of the appellant in
connection  with  Crime  No.  07/2026,
registered at P.S. Crime Branch, District
Bhopal. 
5. The  submission  on  behalf  of  the
1

## Page 499

appellant is that the allegations against
the appellant are in respect of forging a
firm’s letter for opening an account for
transfer  of  funds  of  the  firm.  It  is
submitted that firstly, there is no forensic
evidence to establish that the letter had
been forged; secondly, the remittances are
alleged to be over a period of four years
therefore, the First Information Report is
delayed. Besides, considering the nature of
the offences and the period of incarceration
already suffered by the appellant, it is a
fit  case  where  the  appellant  should  be
released on bail pending trial. 
6. The  learned  Counsel  for  the  State-
respondent as well as the Complainant have
opposed the prayer for bail.
7. We have accorded due consideration to
the rival submissions, without expressing
any opinion on the merits of the prosecution
case,  having  regard  to  the  nature  of
2

## Page 500

offences  and  period  of  pending  trial
incarceration, we are of the view that the
appellant is entitled to be released on bail
pending trial. 
8. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. The
order passed by the High Court rejecting the
regular bail prayer of the appellant is set
aside.
9. The appellant shall be released on
bail on such terms and conditions as the
trial court may deem fit to impose in the
facts and circumstances of the case.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall
stand disposed of.

                   Mr. Rahul K. Gupta, Adv.
                   Mr. Abhigyat Chaitanya, Adv.
                                    
     UPON hearing the counsel, the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The petitioner, Vishwa Bharti, was appointed as Shiksha Mitra.
A challenge was laid to the appointment of multiple Shiksha
Mitras including the petitioner, which was considered by the
Gram Panchayat concerned in its meeting dated 23.04.2008. 
2. Minutes of Meeting would indicate that intermediate pass was
1

## Page 514

SLP(C) No. 12118/2013
the requisite qualification, but the petitioner could manage
an appointment as the Mukhiya of the Panchayat concerned had
given  her  an  opportunity  to  produce  intermediate  pass
certificate within two years. The resolution further indicates
that the petitioner was a close relative of the Mukhiya. 
3. After considering various aspects including what has been
stated  above,  a  resolution  was  passed  cancelling  the
appointment of multiple candidates including the petitioner.
Several candidates filed appeal before the Block Development
Officer1.  Those  appeals  were  decided  vide order  dated
19.08.2008. The petitioner, however, did not prefer an appeal
before the BDO. It appears that the petitioner later preferred
an appeal before the Tribunal, which was constituted in the
meantime. 
4. The Tribunal did not find merit in the appeal and the same was
dismissed. In fact, the Tribunal order also affected other
candidates. The petitioner along with the others filed a writ
petition before the High Court impugning the order passed by
the Tribunal. 
5. During the pendency of the writ petition, the petitioner,
however, withdrew her petition. The petition(s) of the other
candidates was heard and was allowed by the High Court on the
ground that when the BDO had decided the appeal, the Tribunal
could not have sat over the appellate order.
6. At this stage, the petitioner filed a separate writ petition
1  For short ‘BDO’
2

## Page 515

SLP(C) No. 12118/2013
before the High Court, which came to be dismissed by the
learned Single Judge of the High Court,  vide order dated
30.03.2012, holding that the claim of the petitioner for
appointment as Panchayat Teacher by way of absorption from the
post of Shiksha Mitra cannot be entertained, as she had
already been removed from the post of Shiksha Mitra. 
7. Aggrieved by the order passed by the learned Single Judge of
the High Court, the petitioner preferred an intra-court appeal
before the Division Bench of the High Court.  The Division
Bench, by a short order, took the view that since the writ
appellants did not continue as Shiksha Mitra, there  was no
question of her being considered for appointment by way of
absorption as Panchayat Teacher. Consequently, the writ appeal
was dismissed. 
8. Aggrieved by the dismissal of her writ petition and the order
affirming the dismissal of the writ petition, the petitioner
has filed this petition.  
9. The contention of the learned counsel for the petitioner is
that the petitioner is similarly situated as other candidates
whose appeals were allowed by the BDO and later, their writ
petitions against the order of the Tribunal were also allowed.
10. In such circumstances, the petitioner was entitled for similar
treatment. However, the High Court fell in error in dismissing
her writ petition on the ground that the order of the removal
had not been challenged. 
3

## Page 516

SLP(C) No. 12118/2013
11. The learned counsel for the respondent had submitted that
though  there  was  a  common  resolution  cancelling  the
appointment of the petitioner and other candidates, the other
candidates  had  challenged  the  cancellation  order  and
succeeded upto the level of the BDO, whereas the petitioner
had not challenged the said order therefore, she cannot claim
any benefit of the order of the BDO. Further, the subsequent
challenge to the order of the Tribunal was withdrawn by the
petitioner; whereas, the other candidates had pursued their
writ petition. In such circumstances, the order cancelling her
appointment as Shiksha Mitra had attained finality and the
same could not have been challenged later when the post of the
Shiksha Mitra was converted to one of the Panchayat Teacher.
It has been argued that the order passed by the High Court is,
therefore, correct and there is no ground to interfere with
the same. 
12. We have considered the rival submissions and perused the
records carefully. A perusal of the resolution passed by the
Panchayat, cancelling the appointment, would indicate that the
petitioner  did  not  hold  the  requisite  qualification  of
intermediate pass rather she was given liberty to submit
intermediate pass certificate within two years. 
13. The resolution also records the relationship between the
petitioner and the Panchayat Mukhiya. Besides, it appears
from  the  resolution  of  the  Panchayat  that  a  different
4

## Page 517

SLP(C) No. 12118/2013
procedure than what was prescribed by the rules was adopted
for making selections. 
14. No doubt, the other candidates have got the benefit of the
order passed by the BDO, but it is clear from the order of the
BDO that its benefit was not available to the petitioner, as
it was limited to those who were in appeal before him. 
15. Further, the challenge laid to the order of the Tribunal,
whereunder the tribunal sat over the order passed by the BDO,
was withdrawn by the petitioner though the other candidates
got the benefit of the said order. 
16. In  the  aforesaid  circumstances,  once  the  order  of
cancellation of the appointment had attained finality, the
benefit of absorption to the post of Panchayat Teacher from
the post of Shiksha Mitra was not available to the petitioner.
We, therefore, find no merits in this special leave petition
and the same is dismissed. 
17. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Heard Mr. Anand Padmanabhan, learned Senior Counsel for
the petitioner(s), Mr. Harmeet Singh Ruprah, learned counsel
for  the  respondent-State  and  Mr.  Padmesh  Mishra,  learned
counsel for the defacto-complainant.

## Page 524

2
2. The present petitions call in question the correctness of
the  common  impugned  order(s)  dated  07-04-2026  in  MCRC
No.35524/2025 & MCRC No. 34612/2025 passed by the High Court of
Madhya Pradesh Principal Seat at Jabalpur.
3. The  petitioner  was  arrayed  as  an  accused  in  FIR
No.35/2023 dated 07.03.2023 for the offences punishable under
Sections 420, 467, 468 and 471 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860
(for short, 'IPC'). The petitioner was taken into custody on
02.03.2024 and chargesheet was filed on 16.03.2024. The case
against the petitioner is that the petitioner sold part of land
in Khasra No.946/8 to the defacto-complainant for a sale
consideration of Rs.4,00,000/-. It is the case of the defacto-
complainant that the petitioner had no title on the suit
property in question.
4. Originally, the petitioner was granted bail on 11.11.2024
by the High Court inter alia on the condition that entire sale
consideration/defalcated amount be deposited in the concerned
Trial Court and the prosecution will have the liberty to seek
cancellation of bail, if petitioner was found involved in any
other case.
5. Subsequently, on 12.06.2025 an FIR bearing No.197/25 was
registered on the complaint of one Premnarayan @ Prem. On the
basis of this FIR, on 28.07.2025, the defacto-complainant filed
MCRC No.34612/2025 under Section 439(2) read with Section 482
of the Code of Criminal Procedure (for short, ‘CRPC’) seeking
cancellation of bail granted to the petitioner. The State also
filed MCRC No.35524/2025 for the same relief. In the meantime,

## Page 525

3
charge sheet was filed in the subsequent case on 19.09.2025 and
petitioner was enlarged on bail in the said case in connection
with FIR 197/2025, on 22.01.2026. The High Court had cancelled
the bail under the order(s) impugned.
6. When the matter(s) came up for hearing on 05.05.2026,
this Court had stayed the impugned order(s) dated 07.04.2026.
The net result of this was that the petitioner was never taken
back into custody.
7. It is not disputed that the civil case is pending.
Learned Senior Counsel for the petitioner contends that at the
time when the petitioner was granted bail, petitioner had
already  undergone  about  10  months  in  custody;  that  the
petitioner had deposited the entire sale consideration before
the concerned Trial Court; that the criminal antecedents which
has now been sought to be raised, was noticed by the High Court
in the order dated 11.11.2024 whereby bail was granted to the
petitioner.
8. Considering the nature of the offences committed, learned
Senior Counsel submits that having undergone about 10 months in
custody by the petitioner, ends of justice will be served, if
the impugned order(s) is set aside and the original bail order
sustained. Learned Senior Counsel contends that the subsequent
case was registered against the petitioner is also at the
behest of the defacto-complainant in this matter(s) since the
witness(es) is/are common. 
9. Learned counsel for the State and the defacto-complainant
vehemently oppose the submissions of the learned Senior Counsel

## Page 526

4
for the petitioner.
10. Learned counsel for the defacto-complainant submits that
though as part of the contention, the 18 criminal antecedents
have been noticed, it does not form part of the reasoning or of
the consideration of the order granting bail to the petitioner.
11. Learned counsel for the State submits that out of the 18
antecedents pending against the petitioner, some are at the
stage of trial.
12. Having considered the overall facts and circumstances of
the case; considering the nature of offences in the original
FIR, namely FIR No.35/2023 dated 07.03.2023 and the averments
in  the  chargesheet  in  the  said  FIR  and  considering  the
subsequent offence(s) alleged, we are of the opinion that this
is not the case where the High Court should have cancelled the
order of bail.
13. As to whether the defacto-complainant had role in lodging
the second FIR, are all matters for the trial.
14. Insofar as the antecedents are concerned, we have perused
the chart produced by the petitioner. In most of the cases,
acquittal have been recorded.
15. Keeping  in  mind  the  allegation  with  regard  to  the
antecedents and at the same time, keeping in mind the nature of
offences and the fact that the offences under the original FIR
herewith, are triable by the Magistrate concerned, we are
inclined to set aside the impugned order(s). Consequence will
be that the original bail order dated 11.11.2024 will stand
revived and the petitioner will continue on bail on the same

## Page 527

5
conditions of that order. However, we observe that, if the
petitioner is found indulging in any criminal activities,
severe consequence will ensue. 
16. With the above observations, the special leave petitions
are disposed of.
17. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 5612 OF  2026
(Arising out of SLP (Crl) No.13951 of 2025)
Munshiram                                                                ...Appellant
Versus
Dharampal Singh & Ors.                                          ...Respondents
O R D E R
Leave granted.
2. The appellant, the father of a suicidee, is aggrieved with the
impugned order of the High Court of Judicature for Rajasthan, Bench at
Jaipur, which interfered with the cognizance taken by the Trial Court
and remanded it for fresh consideration.
3. We heard Sri Manish K Bishnoi, learned Senior Counsel for the
appellant and Ms. Nidhi Jaswal, learned AoR for the respondent-State.
The party respondents, though, served, have not entered appearance.
4. Admittedly,  earlier,  at  the  stage  of  investigation,  the  party
respondents had  approached  the High  Court  with  a  petition  under
Section 482 of Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, which was allowed,
upon which, the appellant herein had filed the Special Leave Petition
before  this  Court,  disposed  of  by  Annexure  P17  judgment  dated
09.04.2018. Therein, the appellant had pointed out the Suicide Notes

## Page 550

2
and the FSL report, endorsing it to be genuine, to contend that there
was a  prima facie  case made out. This Court, after extracting the
suicide  notes,  held  that  since  the  inquiry  was  pending,  the
investigation should be carried out and taken to its logical conclusion. 
5. Again before the Trial Court, when cognizance was taken and
after  examination  of three witnesses,  the impugned  judgment was
passed remanding the matter for fresh consideration of cognizance.
The High Court had noticed that it was merely based on the cases
initiated by the party respondents that the criminal prosecution was
launched on the ground of abetment; which would not stand scrutiny.
We also find that in the earlier round, the High Court had considered
the wayward ways of the deceased, which was also admitted in a
compromise affidavit.  
6. In any event, since three witnesses were already examined, the
High Court ought not to have set aside the cognizance taken by the
Trial Court. Just as the investigation was taken to its logical conclusion,
now  the  trial  also  should  be  allowed  to  be  proceeded  with  and
culminated either in conviction or acquittal. 
7. Hence, the impugned order dated 25.03.2025 is set aside.
8. We may not be found to have expressed anything on the merits
of the case and we merely noticed the allegations and the counter
allegations.  In  fact,  even  the  earlier  judgment  of  this  Court  at

## Page 551

3
Annexure P17 cannot regulate the trial, since the said observations
were  made  on  a  prima  facie  consideration,  at  the  time  when  the
investigation itself was pending. The Trial Court shall not be influenced
by any observations made by the High Court or this Court on both the
occasions. The contentions of both the parties are left open.
9. The appeal stands allowed.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.

Sections 316(2), 318(4), 338, 336(3), 308(2) and

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.            OF 2026
(ARISING OUT OF SLP (CRIMINAL) NO. 3451 OF 2022
NUSRAT     APPELLANT
VERSUS
THE STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH     RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the parties and perused
the material available on record.
3. By order dated 08.08.2022, this Court had suspended the
sentence and directed release of the appellant on such terms and
conditions as may be fixed by the Trial Court. This Court had
further recorded its dissatisfaction with the inquiries conducted on
behalf of the State of Uttar Pradesh and accordingly directed the
Juvenile  Justice  Board  to  conduct  an  appropriate  inquiry  and
submit a report within three months.
4. Pursuant to the said direction, the Juvenile Justice Board,
Moradabad, conducted a thorough inquiry after giving notice and
affording an opportunity to the State as well as the complainant.
Upon conclusion of the inquiry, the Board held that the appellant
1

## Page 598

was aged 16 years, 10 months and 10 days on the date of the
incident.  The  date  of  birth  claimed  by  the  appellant  i.e.
01.07.1971, was found to be correct. Accordingly, on the date of
the incident, i.e. 11.05.1988, the appellant was less than 18 years
of age. 
5. The appellant, along with his father, was prosecuted for an
offence punishable under Section 307 of the Indian Penal Code,
1860  (IPC)  and  were  convicted  and  sentenced  to  seven  years
rigorous  imprisonment.  The  father  of  the  appellant  has  since
passed away.
6. Learned counsel appearing for the appellant submits that
the appellant has already undergone a little over seven months of
incarceration. In view of the finding declaring the appellant to be
juvenile  on  the  date  of  the  incident,  it  is  submitted  that  the
sentence awarded to him may be modified to the period already
undergone, having regard to the provision of the Juvenile Justice
Act, 1986.
7. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case and
the findings recorded by the Juvenile Justice Board, Moradabad,
while confirming conviction, we modify the sentence imposed upon
the appellant to the period already undergone.
8. The appellant has already been released on bail pursuant
to orders passed by this Court, as noted above. His bail bonds and
sureties shall stand discharged.
9. The appeal stands partly allowed in the above terms. 
2

CIVIL APPEAL NO.         OF 2026

RAVI PRAKASH MISHRA APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
NATIONAL INSURANCE CO. LTD. & 
ANR.
RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The appellant was employed as a security guard with Respondent
No. 2, M/s Adventure Security Services Pvt. Ltd. He suffered 100%
permanent disability in an accident on 17.02.2006, while riding a
motorcycle  owned  by  Respondent  No.  2  in  the  course  of  his
employment. By Award dated 27.02.2018 in MACT Case No. 449279/2016,
the Tribunal awarded him compensation of Rs. 6,88,000/-, with
interest at 9% per annum from 15.03.2010, payable by Respondent
No. 1, the insurance company.
3. On appeal by the insurance company, the High Court of Delhi,
by the impugned judgment dated 02.11.2023 in MAC.APP. No. 576/2018,
held that the appellant, being an employee of the owner, was not a
third party. It further held that the insurer's liability under the
policy was limited to Rs. 1,00,000/-, and reduced the compensation
accordingly.
4. We note that, before the Special Lok Adalat on 01.08.2024, the
insurance company had fairly agreed to restoration of the Award
passed by the Tribunal.
1

## Page 610

5. The appeal is allowed. The impugned judgment is set aside, and
the Award dated 27.02.2018 is restored.
6. The  amount  deposited  by  the  insurance  company  with  the
Tribunal, to the extent not already released, shall be disbursed to
the appellant. Any shortfall shall be deposited by the insurance
company within four weeks.
7. The insurance company shall be at liberty to recover the
amount so paid (in excess of its liability under the policy) from
Respondent No. 2, the owner of the vehicle, in accordance with law.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Criminal Appeal No(s).     /2026
@SLP (Crl.) No(s).   16513/2026
LAXMAN PRAJAPATI @ CHIGURDI                        Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
STATE OF U.P & ORS.                                Respondent(s)
O R D E R 
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. This appeal arises from an order dated 08.05.2026 passed
by the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad whereby the
application of the appellant seeking suspension of sentence
awarded by the trial court pending consideration of his
appeal, has been rejected. 
4. The submission of the learned counsel for the appellant
is that there are various arguable points in the appeal such
as: the First Information Report was lodged with a delay of
about three months; second, the victim, her elder sister and
her mother did not support the prosecution case in its
entirety; and third, the statement of the victim initially was
not  supportive  of  the  prosecution  case  thereafter  she
1

## Page 618

supported the prosecution case and finally she again did not
support the prosecution case. In such circumstances, it is
submitted  that  the  appellant  has  chances  of  acquittal.
Besides, he has spent about four years of incarceration as
against the sentence of 12 years. It is submitted that there
is no likelihood of appeal being decided in near future as it
is of the year 2026.
5. The learned counsel for the respondent-State has opposed
the prayer for suspension of sentence and submitted that the
medical evidence clearly discloses that there was insertion of
a plastic cap into the private part of the victim. Such
insertion  indicates  commission  of  an  offence.  In  such
circumstances, the view taken by the trial court that the
victim turned hostile on account of external pressures is a
plausible view and, therefore, the benefit of suspension of
sentence must not be accorded to the appellant.  
6. We  have  accorded  due  consideration  to  the  rival
submissions, having regard to the nature of the evidence
brought on record as also that the appellant has suffered
incarceration for a period of four years and there is no
likelihood of the appeal being heard in near future, without
expressing any opinion on the merits of the appeal pending
before the High Court, we are of the view that the appellant
is entitled for suspension of sentence pending consideration
2

## Page 619

of his appeal against the trial court’s judgment. 
7. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. The order of the High
Court rejecting the prayer of the appellant to suspend the
sentence pending consideration of his appeal is set aside. The
sentence awarded by the trial court shall remain suspended
pending consideration of appellant’s appeal by the High Court.
8. During pendency of the appeal, the appellant shall be
released on bail on such terms and conditions as the trial
court may deem fit to impose in the facts and circumstances of
the case. 
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

………………………………………………………………..J

New Delhi;

   CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.488 OF 2019

                                VERSUS

O R D E R
Heard Mr. Tripurari Ray, learned counsel for the appellant
and Mr. Sanchit Garga, learned counsel for the respondent-State
of Karnataka.
2. We have heard the matter on merits extensively.
3. Learned counsel for the parties have also assisted the Court
on the basis of the records of the Courts below and the
testimony of the witnesses.
4. Having considered the matter in its entirety, we find that
the view taken by the High Court of Karnataka at Bangalore in
its impugned judgment dated 13.10.2011 in Criminal Appeal No.342
of  2006  is  the  correct  view  and  the  reasons  for  having
overturned the acquittal of the appellant by the High Court
appears to be cogent based on the materials available before the
High Court and what had come during the trial. The approach by
the Trial Court appears to be lopsided and rightly the High
Court has corrected the wrong appreciation of the facts based on

## Page 626

2
the evidence adduced and other materials available before the
High Court.
5. Accordingly, we find no merit in the present appeal and the
same stands dismissed.
6. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

NATIONAL INSURANCE CO. LTD.    RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The present appeal arises out of the impugned
order dated 19.03.2024 passed by the High Court of
Orissa at Cuttack in MACA No. 1086 of 2023.
3. The facts of the case reveal that on account
of the death of the father of the petitioner(s) in
an accident, a sum of Rs. 80,08,160/- was awarded
as  compensation  by  the  Motor  Accidents  Claims
Tribunal. However, on appeal, the said amount was
reduced by the High Court to the tune of Rs.
66,12,350/-.
4. Learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
1

## Page 634

appellant(s)  has  vehemently  argued  before  this
Court that the salary of the deceased was not
rightly taken into account by the High Court and
the  compensation  amount  was  reduced  without
assigning any cogent reason. It has also been
argued  that  during  the  pendency  of  the  claim
petition, as some of the dependents expired, the
High Court erroneously reduced the compensation
amount by altering the deduction towards personal
expenses from one-fourth to one-third.
5. Having heard learned counsel for the parties
and upon perusal of the record, this Court is of
the considered opinion that the High Court ought
not to have reduced the compensation amount merely
because some of the claimants expired during the
pendency of the proceedings.
6. In the considered opinion of this Court, the
compensation awarded by the Motor Accidents Claims
Tribunal deserves to be restored, and therefore,
the compensation of Rs. 80,08,160/- awarded by the
MACT is hereby restored. 
7. If the said balance amount has not already
2

## Page 635

been paid, the same shall be deposited/paid within
a period of two months from today.
8. Further, the right granted to the respondent-
Insurance  Company  to  pay  and  recover  the
compensation amount shall continue to operate in
accordance with law.
9. With the aforesaid modification, the appeal
stands disposed of.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

FAROOQ AHMAD                                       Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
STATE OF JAMMU AND KASHMIR                         Respondent(s)
IA No. 291513/2026 - CONDONATION OF DELAY IN FILING
 
Date : 25-11-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM :  HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE M.M. SUNDRESH
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE PRASANNA B. VARALE
For Petitioner(s) :Ms. Rukhsana Choudhury- 1545, AOR (VC)
                   Ms. Shumaila, Adv.
                                      
For Respondent(s) :Mr. Parth Awasthi, Adv. 
Mr. Pashupathi Nath Razdan, AOR - 2054  
Upon hearing the counsel, the Court made the following
O R D E R
1. Leave granted. 
2. The appellant has been convicted for the offences
punishable under Sections 302 and 307 of the Jammu and
Kashmir State Ranbir Penal Code, 1989 (for short, ‘the
RPC’) in connection with File No.03-A/Sessions Challan
arising out of F.I.R. No. 222 of 2000, registered at
Police  Station-Bhaderwah,  District-Doda,  Jammu  &
1

## Page 642

Kashmir and has been sentenced to undergo rigorous
imprisonment for life with fine.  The High Court, while
affirming the conviction and sentence of the Trial
Court,  dismissed  the  appeal  of  the  appellant  vide
impugned  order  dated  26.09.2022,  passed  in  CRA
No.9900001/2015, Crl.M No.395/2022 c/w Crl.Ref(L) No.
04/2022.   Aggrieved,  the  appellant  is  before  this
Court. 
3. The learned counsel appearing for the appellant
submits  that  the  appellant  was  not  arrayed  as  an
accused in the F.I.R. and has been implicated pursuant
to further investigation. The learned counsel further
submits  that  the  appellant  has  already  undergone
incarceration for a period of more than twenty years
with remission. 
4. The case of the prosecution in a nutshell is that
the appellant along with the other accused person(s),
after hatching a conspiracy, barged into the house of
the deceased and PW-2, with arms and ammunition, and
fired indiscriminately upon them in order to commit
their murder. 
5. The learned counsel appearing for the respondent-
State would submit that it is not correct to state that
there were three accused.  In fact, there were only two
2

## Page 643

accused,  of  which  the  other  accused  had  died  on
01.11.2000 in an encounter with the STF.
6. It is further submitted that the fact that there
was no recovery of weapon at the instance of the
appellant and that he was thereafter acquitted of the
charge under Sections 7/27 of the Arms Act, 1959, would
not  enure  to  the  benefit  of  the  appellant,
notwithstanding the fact that he has not been charged
for the offence punishable under Section 120-B of the
Indian Penal Code, 1860.
7. We have heard the learned counsel appearing for
the parties and perused the material placed on record. 
8. On a perusal of the record, it reveals that there
is some evidence to show that there are more than two
accused involved. As there was no recovery against the
appellant, he has been acquitted of the charges under
the Arms Act, 1959.  The evidentiary value of PW-4
(father of the deceased) and other witnesses, would
have to be assessed at the time of hearing the appeal.
9. Suffice it to state that the appellant has been
under incarceration for more than twenty years with
remission, and the incident occurred way back in the
year 2000 and hence, more than 25 years have elapsed
3

## Page 644

since the date of the incident.  
10. In view of the abovesaid facts and circumstances
of the present case, and taking into consideration the
period of incarceration, we suspend the sentence of the
appellant  and  grant  him  bail  on  the  terms  and
conditions, to the satisfaction of the concerned Trial
Court during the pendency of the present appeal. 
11. List the appeal for hearing in its due course. 
12. In the meantime, the records from the Courts below
may be called for. 
 (SHUBHAM SONI)                              (POONAM VAID)
COURT MASTER (SH)                         ASSISTANT  REGISTRAR

For Respondent(s) : Mr. Balaji Srinivasan- 1546, AOR

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. We were surprised as to how a Public Interest Litigation
was  taken  up  by  the  High  Court  of  Judicature  at
Allahabad, at Lucknow to regulate the elections to the
Governing Body of the Oudh Bar Association.

## Page 674

2
2. Sri Jaideep Gupta, learned Senior Counsel appearing for
the  petitioner  herein  submits  that  his  instructing
Counsel  informed  him  that  the  petitioners  have
acknowledged the election to the Oudh Bar Association
held on 28.10.2026, the results of which were declared on
29.10.2026. The elected members have taken charge after
certificates were distributed by the Elders Committee of
the Oudh Bar Association, High Court at Lucknow Bench.
Though, the directions issued cannot be sustained, in the
circumstances noticed above, it has been resolved as
hereinabove stated by the Elders Committee of the Oudh
Bar Association that while not giving up the challenge
against the order itself, there is no challenge to the
election.
3. As we noticed, we are surprised as to how the PIL was
taken up to regulate the elections to the Bar Association
in which directions were issued to eliminate certain
persons  who  did  not  have  certificate  of  practice,
especially without hearing them and directions issued to
the High Court on the Administrative side, to take
cognizance of the ensuing elections and ensure that the
outsiders and persons not entitled to vote are not
allowed to enter into the area where the election is to
take place.
4. First of all, the elections to the Bar Association could
not have been regulated by the judicial orders passed by
the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution of
India; especially in a PIL, when the petitioner, who is
an Advocate cannot be said to be representing the cause
of people who are marginalized or who do not have access
to the Courts.

## Page 675

3
5. We were about to close the proceedings, making the above
observations, when some interveners appeared and took up
cudgels  against  individual  candidates  and  the  votes
polled and so on and so forth. We were of the opinion
that nothing of that sort could be entertained by this
Court; especially when we find the entertainment of the
PIL  itself  to  be  misplaced.  We  find  no  reason  to
entertain the petition seeking intervention and all of
such intervention applications shall stand rejected.
6. With the above observation, we close the SLP recording
the submission of the petitioner that the elected Office
Bearers of the Association have taken charge.
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.
 (VISHAL ANAND)                                    (POOJA SHARMA)
DEPUTY REGISTRAR                                 COURT MASTER (NSH)

   UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                          O R D E R
1. SLP (C) No. 40080 of 2026 is taken on board.  
2. As per our orders dated 18.11.2026 and 20.11.2026 passed in
SLP (C) Nos. 40024/2026, 40063/2026, 40064/2026, 40080/2026 and
40250/2026, we had directed that the petitioner – colleges shall be
permitted to participate in on-going counselling (stray round).
3. It appears that due to some technical issue, these colleges
could not participate in the counselling.
4. In the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case, we direct
that a Special Stray Round shall be conducted exclusively for these
colleges. In the event the students opt for admission in these
colleges, each of the students shall be issued a letter by the
National Commission for Indian System of Medicine (‘Commission’)
individually, indicating that no right of admission will be created
in their favour and that their admission will be subject to the
disposal of the appeal, which may be filed by Commission.
5. It is made clear that our order has no bearing on any further
action that the Commission might take in view of any deficiency
that they may detect.
6. As stated supra, we have passed this order in the peculiar
facts and circumstances of the case, and this order shall not be
treated as a precedent and no High Court shall pass any order based

## Page 678

on the directions given in this order.  
7. With these observations, the Special Leave Petitions are
disposed of.
8. Pending interlocutory application(s), if any, is/are disposed
of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the

O R D E R
I.A. No.351323/2026 in Crl. A. No.4401/2026:
The applicant/appellant - Mahesh has been
convicted  for  the  offences  punishable  under
Sections 302 and 201 of the Indian Penal Code,
1860 and was sentenced to undergo imprisonment for
life, along with fine and default stipulations.
The judgment of conviction and order on sentence
rendered by the Trial Court, has been confirmed by
the  High  Court.  Aggrieved  by  the  same,  the
applicant/appellant - Mahesh is before this Court.
The applicant/appellant - Mahesh has been
under actual incarceration for a period of nearly
10 years and the sentence imposed on the co-
accused has already been suspended. 
Considering  the  aforesaid  position,  and
taking  note  of  the  pendency  of  the  present
appeal, which is not likely to be taken up for
hearing anytime soon, we are inclined to suspend
the  sentence  and  grant  bail  to  the
applicant/appellant - Mahesh.
Accordingly, the sentence imposed upon
2

## Page 687

the  applicant/appellant  -  Mahesh stands
suspended, and he is granted bail during the
pendency of the present appeal, subject to the
terms and conditions that may be imposed by the
concerned Trial Court.
The application stands allowed, accordingly.
List  the  appeal(s)  for  hearing  in  due
course.

of the respondent-State of Bihar. Hence, formal notice is
waived.

only.

petitioner shall be released on bail in connection with
Complaint Case No. 21 of 2023, registered at Nasariganj
Police Station, District Rohtas, Bihar, on his furnishing
a personal bond in the sum of Rs.25,000/- (Rupees Twenty-
Five Thousand Only), with one or more sureties in the
like amount, to the satisfaction of the Investigating
Officer.

investigation and report to the Investigating Officer as
and when directed to do so.

Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned senior counsel for the appellant
and learned Additional Solicitor General(ASG) for respondent-
Union of India. 
3. The only grievance of the appellant is with regard to the
condition imposed on him namely, ‘not to leave the jurisdiction
of the New Town Police Station, Kolkata’. The appellant hails
from Madhubani, Bihar. He submitted that the said condition may
be relaxed inasmuch as he is already cooperating with the trial
and it is stated that five out of eleven witnesses have been
examined. 
4. Learned senior counsel also submitted that if the said
condition is relaxed or set aside, the appellant would ensure
his presence before the Special Court on every date of hearing
without fail.
5. In response to this submission, learned ASG contended
that if this Court is inclined to relax and set aside the said
condition then a strict direction may be imposed on the
appellant to attend every date of hearing failing which the
Special Court may take steps to cancel his bail. 
1

## Page 701

6. We have noted the submissions advanced at the bar. 
7. Consequently,  we  relax  and  set  aside  the  condition
imposed on the appellant ‘not to leave the jurisdiction of the
New Town Police Station’. However the appellant shall be
present on every date of hearing before the Special Court and
in the event he fails to appear on any particular date, for no
good reason, then the Special Court may take steps to cancel
the relief of bail granted to the appellant herein after
hearing the appellant.
In view of the above, the Criminal Appeals stand disposed
of.
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. On 20.03.2025 while deciding Civil Appeal No. 1080/2017
titled “State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.vs. Dinesh Kumar Sharma &
Ors.” inter alia following directions were passed:
“20.  In light of the above, the appeal stands
dismissed  except  for  holding  the  respondents
entitled to arrears of pension for a period of
1

## Page 746

three years prior to the date of the filing of
their Writ Petition or the date of attaining the
age 60 years whichever is earlier for the relief
as granted by the High Court. As regards the
benefits  which  have  been  disbursed  to  the
respondents  under  the  Contributory  Pension
Scheme,  the  appellants  would  be  entitled  to
deduct  the  said  amount  from  the  arrears  of
pension payable to the respondents. This exercise
shall be carried out within a period of one
month. In case there is still some amount due to
be paid by the respondents, the said amount shall
be conveyed to the respondents within a period of
two weeks after the expiry of the initial one
month  as  granted,  which  shall  thereafter  be
deposited by the respondents within a period of
two  weeks.  On  doing  so,  the  arrears  and/or
pension as per entitlement would be paid within
thirty days”.
2. For non-compliance with the said direction, the present
contempt petition was filed by the petitioners, who were
respondents in the civil appeal, claiming the benefits that
accrued to them as a consequence of the State's appeal having
been dismissed.
3. Notice was issued in the contempt petition, in which a
reply had been filed by the respondents asserting that because
of the legislation passed by the State Assembly i.e.  Uttar
Pradesh  Entitlement  to  Pension  and  Validation  Act,2025
(U.P.Act No. 5/2026), the liability upon the respondent/State
does not exist as the very basis of the passing of the order
had been taken away.
4. It has been brought to the notice of the Court today
during the hearing that in a bunch of appeals where the
challenge was to the said Validation Act of 2021 and 2025, the
said appeals have been allowed by declaring the said Acts as
ultra vires.  The basis which was taken as a plea for
2

## Page 747

asserting that the contempt would not now lie against the
respondents would, therefore cease to exist.  The directions
in question were issued primarily to the State, and therefore,
the plea taken by the learned senior counsel appearing for the
respondents that the respondents herein are no longer holding
the posts as on the date of the judgment and even today, and
therefore, are not likely to be held liable for contempt.
5. This contention of the learned senior counsel for the
respondents herein appears to carry weight to some extent,
however, the fact remains that the ground previously given for
not giving effect to the judgment/order passed by this Court
dated 20.03.2025 no longer exists.  Accordingly, contempt
would in any case,  lie against the officials, who are holding
the posts at present and the liability of the State under the
said order stands.  Accordingly, with an intent to grant an
opportunity to comply with the order and purge the contempt,
we direct compliance with the order dated 20.03.2025 as stated
in paragraph 20 of the judgment reproduced above, within the
time stipulated therein.
6. It is made clear that in case of non-compliance with the
order within the time stipulated therein, i.e., 10 weeks from
today, the Chief Secretary, State of Uttar Pradesh, and the
Cane Commissioner, Uttar Pradesh shall appear in person before
the Court to face contempt proceedings.
7. Hearing of the case is deferred to 24.02.2027.
(RAJNI MUKHI)                            (MAYA KUMARI)
ASTT. REGISTRAR-cum-PS                  COURT MASTER (NSH)

NATIONAL INSURANCE COMPANY

O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The appellant was injured in a motor accident on 07.04.2015
and suffered 40% permanent disability. By Award dated 12.12.2018,
the  Motor  Accident  Claims  Tribunal,  Shopian,  awarded  him
compensation of Rs. 2,00,000/-. On an appeal by the insurance
company, MA No. 27/2019, the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and
Ladakh at Srinagar passed its judgment dated 27.05.2022. By that
judgment, it reduced the compensation to Rs. 1,20,000/-; reduced
the rate of interest to 6% per annum; directed the appellant to
repay any amount received in excess; and granted  the insurance
company the right to recover the awarded amount from the owner of
the offending vehicle.
3. The appellant's review petition, RP No. 95/2022, was dismissed
by the impugned order dated 19.02.2024. Though the appellant has
assailed only the order dismissing his review petition, we deem it
appropriate, in the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case
and in order to do complete justice between the parties, to examine
the judgment dated 27.05.2022 as well.
1

## Page 758

4. The appeal is allowed. The impugned order dated 19.02.2024 is
set aside. The judgment dated 27.05.2022 is also set aside insofar
as it reduces the compensation and the rate of interest and directs
the  appellant  to  repay  the  excess  amount.  The  Award  dated
12.12.2018 passed by the Tribunal is restored to that extent.
5. Consequently, if compensation in terms of the Award has
already  been  paid,  no  recovery  shall  be  effected  from  the
appellant.  If any amount remains payable under the Award, the
insurance company shall pay the same within four weeks.
6. The right granted to the insurance company by the High Court,
in paragraph 13 of the judgment dated 27.05.2022, to recover the
awarded amount from the owner of the offending vehicle is kept
intact.
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

been violated, necessary consequences will follow.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.       OF 2025
(arising out of SLP(Crl.) No. 3681/2026)
STATE OF RAJASTHAN ..... APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
VIJAY KUMAR SINGHAL ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted. 
2. Challenge in this appeal is to the order dated 07.10.2024
passed by the High Court of Judicature at Rajasthan, Bench at
Jaipur,  in  S.B.  Criminal  Miscellaneous  (Petition)  No.
5351/2023.  The said petition was filed under Section 482 of
the Code of Criminal Procedure, 19731, assailing the prosecution
sanction order dated 23.06.2021.  By the impugned judgment, the
High Court deemed it appropriate to exercise its inherent
jurisdiction to quash the said sanction order. 
3. Significantly, the High Court was apprised of the fact that the
petitioner in the quash petition, the respondent, Vijay Kumar
Singhal, had earlier filed S.B. Criminal Writ Petition No.
643/2022 before the Rajasthan High Court, Bench at Jaipur,
assailing  the  very  same  prosecution  sanction  order  dated
1  ‘Cr.P.C.’ for short
1

## Page 770

Criminal Appeal @ SLP(Crl.) No.3681/2026
23.06.2021  and  the  said  writ  petition  was  dismissed  on
04.07.2023. 
4. Despite noting the said fact, the learned Judge of the High
Court deemed it proper to ignore the same and allowed the quash
petition. We are unable to accept this indulgence. It was not
open  to  the  respondent,  having  already  invoked  the  writ
jurisdiction of the High Court in relation to the prosecution
sanction order to thereafter take recourse to its inherent
jurisdiction under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. in relation to
the very same impugned order. This was clearly an abuse of
process and the High Court ought to have been mindful of this
fact while dealing with the matter. 
5. The  failure  on  the  part  of  the  learned  Judge  to  do  so
constrains  us  to  set  aside  the  impugned  judgment  dated
07.10.2024 passed in S.B. Criminal Miscellaneous (Petition) No.
5351/2023.
6. The appeal is, accordingly, allowed in the aforestated terms. 
7. All issues are left open to be raised before the trial Court. 
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

1. Leave granted. 
2. The issue as regards the retrospective application of the
Arbitration and Conciliation (Amendment) Act, 2019, whereby
Section 29-A of the  Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 19961,
was amended in August, 2019, stands settled by the decision of
this Court in ‘Tata Sons Private Limited (formerly Tata Sons
Limited)  vs.  Siva  Industries  and  Holdings  Limited  and
Others2’, wherein this Court observed that, as the amendment
to Section 29-A(1) in the year 2019 was remedial in nature, it
should be applicable to all the pending arbitral proceedings
as on the effective date, that is, 30.08.2019. 
3. This aspect of the matter stands settled against the appellant
but we find that the Commercial Court at Gangtok, while
considering the application filed by the appellant under
Section 34 of the 1996 Act in Commercial (Arbitration) Case
1  ‘the 1996 Act’ for short
2  (2023) 5 SCC 421
1

## Page 773

No. 05 of 2023, deemed it appropriate to dispose of the same
on the short ground of limitation in the context of Section
29-A of the 1996 Act and did not consider the other grounds
raised therein on merits.
4. As the High Court deemed it appropriate to restore the award
in the appeal filed by the respondent under Section 37 of the
1996 Act only on that short ground, we are of the opinion that
the other grounds raised by the appellant in the application
filed  under  Section  34  of  the  1996  Act  require  to  be
considered on their own merits and in accordance with law.  As
the Court concerned failed to undertake that exercise, we
allow  this  appeal  in  part,  by  restoring  Commercial
(Arbitration)  Case  No.  05  of  2023  on  the  file  of  the
Commercial Court at Gangtok for consideration afresh on merits
and in accordance with law. 
5. All issues, apart from the issue covered by the decision of
this Court in Tata Sons Private Limited (supra), are left open
to be considered therein.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The  petitioner before  this Court  has filed  the
1

## Page 794

present petition, being aggrieved by the impugned order
dated 26.03.2026 passed by the High Court of Kerala at
Ernakulam in Bail Application No. 1546 of 2026, rejecting
the  prayer  for  anticipatory  bail  in  connection  with
FIR/Crime No. 86 of 2026, registered at Police Station
Vythiri,  District  Wayanad,  Kerala,  for  the  offences
punishable  under  Sections  318(4)  and  316(2)  of  the
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
2. Vide order dated 11.06.2026, this Court had granted
interim protection from arrest to the petitioner. Pursuant
thereto, the petitioner was called by the Investigating
Officer and has duly appeared before him twice to join the
investigation.
3. However, the contention of learned counsel for the
respondent-State is that the petitioner has not disclosed
the whereabouts of the other co-accused persons and has not
produced the original Memorandum of Understanding (MoU).
Learned counsel appearing for the complainant has also
vehemently opposed the prayer for grant of anticipatory
bail,  submitting  that  the  petitioner  has  duped  the
complainant and, therefore, no case for anticipatory bail
is made out.
4. This Court after hearing learned counsel for the
parties and keeping in view the totality of circumstances,
2

## Page 795

is of the opinion that the interim order dated 11.06.2026
deserves to be made absolute.
6. Accordingly, interim order dated 11.06.2026 is made
absolute subject to the condition that petitioner shall
continue to co-operate with the investigation and shall
report  as  and  when  called  upon  to  do  so  by  the
Investigating Authority.
7. The Special Leave Petition is accordingly disposed
of in the above terms.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.

undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of two years,

order dated 05.02.2026 passed by this Court has been duly
complied with and that a sum of Rs. 2,00,00,000/- (Rupees
Two Crores only) has been deposited in the Registry of this
Court.
3. On  the  other  hand,  learned  counsel  for  the
respondent-State has vehemently opposed the prayer for
suspension of sentence. 
4. Having  heard  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
parties  and  taking  into  consideration  the  facts  and
circumstances of the case, this Court is of the considered
view that the petitioner has made out a case for suspension
of sentence. Accordingly, the prayer for suspension of
2

## Page 801

sentence is allowed.
5. Consequently,  the  execution  of  the  substantive
sentence of imprisonment imposed upon the petitioner shall
remain suspended during the pendency of the Special Leave
Petitions.  The  petitioner  shall  be  released  on  bail,
subject to such terms and conditions as may be imposed by
the Trial Court, provided he is not required to be detained
in connection with any other case.
6. Let  fresh  notice  be  issued  to  the  unserved
complainant. Learned counsel appearing for the petitioner
shall take appropriate steps to effect service within a
period of two weeks.
7. The amount deposited in the Registry of this Court
shall be kept in an interest-bearing Fixed Deposit Receipt

done.

rary Release) Act, 1962, at Police Station Division

convict under POCSO was released on parole on
06.11.2023 for a period of one month, however, that
he did not return to prison after the expiry of pa-

order to evade lawful custody, in conspiracy with
his family members, and certain members of the Gram
Panchayat fabricated his own death by procuring a
false death certificate and submitting it to the
jail authorities through his sister. Thereafter,
Himanshu allegedly assumed the identity of one
Sunil and continued to reside under the said ficti-
tious  identity.  The  Petitioner  herein  is  the
elected Panch of Village Mubarkpur where the co-ac-
cused Himanshu resided, and the allegation against
him is that he issued the alleged death certificate
in conspiracy with the family members of co-accused
Himanshu.

that it is admitted that the alleged death certifi-
cate was issued by the Petitioner only on the basis
of the supporting documents submitted before him.
